It always presents with Charcot's triad
It is defined by the presence of a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
originalOptions: It requires a common bile duct dilated below 5-7 mm
It always presents with Charcot's triad
It is defined by the presence of a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
questions.correctAnswer: D) It is defined by the presence of a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
questions.correctAnswerText: It is defined by the presence of a stone in the common bile duct, and the duct may be normal or dilated
questions.explanation: Choledocholithiasis is defined by stone location (CBD), not by a specific duct diameter cutoff; duct diameter thresholds are age- and context-dependent, and cholangitis is a distinct, more severe infectious complication.

questions.text: Murphy's sign — inspiratory arrest on deep palpation under the right costal margin — is characteristic of which condition?
questions.explanation: Murphy's sign reflects gallbladder inflammation causing pain-induced inspiratory arrest when the inflamed gallbladder contacts the examiner's fingers; it is not a feature of appendicitis, for which psoas/Rovsing signs are used instead.

questions.text: Which term describes infection of the biliary tree, usually occurring behind an obstructed common bile duct?
questions.explanation: Cholangitis is biliary tree infection typically from CBD obstruction (often by a stone), presenting with Charcot's triad (fever, jaundice, RUQ pain), which can progress to Reynolds' pentad with hypotension and altered mental status; this differs from cholecystitis, which is gallbladder inflammation from cystic-duct obstruction.

questions.text: Which statement about Meckel's diverticulum is FALSE?
options: It is more common in females
originalOptions: It is more common in females
questions.correctAnswer: D) It is more common in females
questions.correctAnswerText: It is more common in females
questions.explanation: Meckel diverticulum complications are actually more common in males; ectopic gastric/pancreatic tissue, bleeding, and the "rule of 2s" (2 inches long, 2 feet from the ileocecal valve, ~2% of population) are classic true associations.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT considered an independent predictor of adverse outcome in upper GI bleeding?
questions.explanation: A hematocrit below 45% is not itself a validated adverse-outcome threshold; the recognized poor-prognostic features include hematocrit <30%, SBP <100 mmHg, red blood on NG lavage, and cirrhosis/ascites, since initial hematocrit can lag behind acute blood loss.

questions.text: What does visible blood in a nasogastric aspirate suggest in a patient with GI bleeding?
options: It excludes a lower-GI source definitively
A negative aspirate excludes an upper-GI bleed
It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
It is diagnostic of Mallory-Weiss tear
originalOptions: It excludes a lower-GI source definitively
A negative aspirate excludes an upper-GI bleed
It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
It is diagnostic of Mallory-Weiss tear
questions.correctAnswer: D) It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
questions.correctAnswerText: It supports an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a negative aspirate does not exclude an upper-GI bleed
questions.explanation: A bloody NG aspirate raises suspicion for an upper-GI source and higher-risk bleeding, but a clear aspirate can occur even with active upper-GI bleeding (e.g., duodenal source with pylorospasm), so it cannot rule it out.

questions.text: A patient with chronic alcohol-related liver disease presents with hematemesis. Which source of upper-GI bleeding must be urgently considered?
questions.correctAnswer: C) Esophageal or gastric variceal hemorrhage
questions.explanation: Chronic liver disease predisposes to portal hypertension and variceal bleeding, which requires urgent vasoactive/antibiotic therapy and endoscopy; however, chronic alcohol use alone does not confirm the diagnosis, so other causes should still be considered.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute right lower quadrant pain and McBurney's point tenderness. What is the most likely diagnosis and initial management approach?
options: Acute appendicitis; imaging (ultrasound in children/pregnant women, CT in adults), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
Mesenteric ischemia; immediate CT angiography and heparin
Testicular torsion; urgent urology consult only
Nonspecific abdominal pain; discharge with follow-up
originalOptions: Acute appendicitis; imaging (ultrasound in children/pregnant women, CT in adults), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
Mesenteric ischemia; immediate CT angiography and heparin
Testicular torsion; urgent urology consult only
Nonspecific abdominal pain; discharge with follow-up
questions.correctAnswer: A) Acute appendicitis; imaging (ultrasound in children/pregnant women, CT in adults), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
questions.correctAnswerText: Acute appendicitis; imaging (ultrasound in children/pregnant women, CT in adults), IV fluids/antibiotics, and surgical evaluation
questions.explanation: McBurney's point tenderness in the RLQ is classic for acute appendicitis, prompting confirmatory imaging (modality chosen by age/pregnancy status), supportive care, and prompt surgical evaluation.

questions.text: Which statement about angiodysplasia is correct?
options: It consists of healthy new vessels that never bleed
It is a congenital malformation exclusive to the colon
It consists of fragile, dilated mucosal/submucosal vessels that can cause intermittent GI bleeding
originalOptions: It consists of healthy new vessels that never bleed
It is a congenital malformation exclusive to the colon
It consists of fragile, dilated mucosal/submucosal vessels that can cause intermittent GI bleeding
questions.correctAnswer: D) It consists of fragile, dilated mucosal/submucosal vessels that can cause intermittent GI bleeding
questions.correctAnswerText: It consists of fragile, dilated mucosal/submucosal vessels that can cause intermittent GI bleeding
questions.explanation: Angiodysplasia represents acquired, fragile vascular ectasias prone to intermittent bleeding, most commonly in the cecum/right colon, unlike the false premise that these are healthy, non-bleeding vessels.

questions.text: Which set of features supports a diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain (NSAP) as a diagnosis of exclusion?
options: Peritonism, toxic appearance, and worsening symptoms
Hemodynamic stability, no peritonism/toxic appearance, mild or nonlocalizing tenderness, normal/nondiagnostic investigations, and improving symptoms tolerating oral intake
Positive imaging for a surgical cause
originalOptions: Peritonism, toxic appearance, and worsening symptoms
Hemodynamic stability, no peritonism/toxic appearance, mild or nonlocalizing tenderness, normal/nondiagnostic investigations, and improving symptoms tolerating oral intake
Positive imaging for a surgical cause
questions.correctAnswer: C) Hemodynamic stability, no peritonism/toxic appearance, mild or nonlocalizing tenderness, normal/nondiagnostic investigations, and improving symptoms tolerating oral intake
questions.correctAnswerText: Hemodynamic stability, no peritonism/toxic appearance, mild or nonlocalizing tenderness, normal/nondiagnostic investigations, and improving symptoms tolerating oral intake
questions.explanation: NSAP is a diagnosis of exclusion made after ruling out surgical emergencies; it is characterized by stability, absence of peritoneal signs, nondiagnostic workup, and clinical improvement, with reliable follow-up arranged.

questions.text: What does the cremasteric reflex assess, and what is its clinical significance?
options: Stroking the inner thigh causes ipsilateral testicular elevation via cremaster muscle contraction; it is commonly absent in testicular torsion
Stroking the lateral thigh causes contralateral testicular elevation; it confirms epididymitis
It is elicited by palpating the scrotum directly and is always present in torsion
It has no clinical significance in scrotal pain evaluation
originalOptions: Stroking the inner thigh causes ipsilateral testicular elevation via cremaster muscle contraction; it is commonly absent in testicular torsion
Stroking the lateral thigh causes contralateral testicular elevation; it confirms epididymitis
It is elicited by palpating the scrotum directly and is always present in torsion
It has no clinical significance in scrotal pain evaluation
questions.correctAnswer: A) Stroking the inner thigh causes ipsilateral testicular elevation via cremaster muscle contraction; it is commonly absent in testicular torsion
questions.correctAnswerText: Stroking the inner thigh causes ipsilateral testicular elevation via cremaster muscle contraction; it is commonly absent in testicular torsion
questions.explanation: The cremasteric reflex is often absent with testicular torsion due to cord compromise, but its presence does not exclude torsion, so urgent surgical evaluation should not be delayed when clinical suspicion is high.

questions.text: How should a patient with an Alvarado score of 6 be managed?
options: Immediate discharge with no further workup
Oral antibiotics alone as outpatient therapy
originalOptions: Immediate discharge with no further workup
Oral antibiotics alone as outpatient therapy
questions.explanation: An intermediate (5,6 score) does not reliably confirm or exclude appendicitis, so further imaging and reassessment (rather than discharge or immediate surgery) is the appropriate next step.

questions.text: Among alcohol, gallstones, idiopathic disease, hypertriglyceridemia, and snake bite, which is the LEAST typical cause of acute pancreatitis?
questions.explanation: Gallstones and alcohol are the most common causes of pancreatitis, with hypertriglyceridemia and idiopathic disease also well-established; venom-related pancreatitis is rare and classically associated with scorpion (not snake) envenomation in teaching mnemonics.

questions.text: What is the most common overall cause of acute abdominal pain presenting to the emergency department?
questions.explanation: Nonspecific abdominal pain accounts for the largest proportion (roughly a third) of ED abdominal pain presentations overall, though the most common surgical cause or the leading cause in a specific age group may differ.

questions.text: What is the most significant risk factor for developing an abdominal aortic aneurysm (AAA)?
questions.explanation: Smoking is the strongest modifiable risk factor for AAA; other risk factors include age >65, male sex, hypertension, COPD, family history, and atherosclerosis, whereas diabetes is paradoxically associated with a lower AAA risk.

questions.text: Is mild, nonlocalizing tenderness compatible with a diagnosis of nonspecific abdominal pain?
options: No, NSAP requires a completely painless abdomen
True; NSAP is a diagnosis of exclusion but can include mild, nonlocalizing tenderness
True, but only in pediatric patients
False, tenderness always indicates a surgical cause
originalOptions: No, NSAP requires a completely painless abdomen
True; NSAP is a diagnosis of exclusion but can include mild, nonlocalizing tenderness
True, but only in pediatric patients
False, tenderness always indicates a surgical cause
questions.correctAnswer: C) True; NSAP is a diagnosis of exclusion but can include mild, nonlocalizing tenderness
questions.correctAnswerText: True; NSAP is a diagnosis of exclusion but can include mild, nonlocalizing tenderness
questions.explanation: NSAP can present with mild, nonlocalizing tenderness, but guarding, rigidity, rebound, hemodynamic instability, or a toxic appearance should prompt evaluation for a specific serious cause before the diagnosis of exclusion is made.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a major compartment for occult blood loss causing hemorrhagic shock in an adult?
questions.explanation: Intracranial hemorrhage is neurologically devastating but the closed, limited cranial vault cannot accommodate enough blood loss to cause systemic hemorrhagic shock in an adult, unlike the chest, abdomen/retroperitoneum, pelvis, and long bones.

questions.text: At what age does testicular torsion most commonly occur?
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion peaks during adolescence; while it can occur at any age (so older age doesn't exclude it), only a minority of cases occur after age 20.

questions.text: A patient presents with acute RUQ pain, no fever, and imaging revealing gallstones without other complicating features. What is the next step?
options: Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
originalOptions: Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.correctAnswer: D) Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.correctAnswerText: Analgesia with follow-up for elective cholecystectomy
questions.explanation: Afebrile biliary colic without inflammatory or obstructive features (no Murphy sign, jaundice, or duct dilation) is managed with analgesia and elective surgical follow-up, reserving admission and urgent intervention for complicated disease.

questions.text: Which statement about biliary colic pain is correct?
options: It is specifically triggered only by protein intake
It may radiate to the right shoulder or subscapular region
It always begins exactly 15 minutes after eating
It is relieved specifically by antacids
originalOptions: It is specifically triggered only by protein intake
It may radiate to the right shoulder or subscapular region
It always begins exactly 15 minutes after eating
It is relieved specifically by antacids
questions.correctAnswer: B) It may radiate to the right shoulder or subscapular region
questions.correctAnswerText: It may radiate to the right shoulder or subscapular region
questions.explanation: Biliary colic classically radiates to the right shoulder/subscapular area due to shared phrenic nerve innervation; episodes are commonly precipitated by fatty meals, but timing and triggers vary between patients.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a sign of retroperitoneal hemorrhage?
questions.explanation: Battle sign (mastoid ecchymosis) suggests a basilar skull fracture, not retroperitoneal bleeding; Cullen sign (periumbilical) and Grey Turner sign (flank) are both associated with intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal hemorrhage.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about testicular torsion is WRONG?
options: Rapid growth of the testis may predispose to torsion
Spontaneous detorsion occurs in about 10% of cases
originalOptions: Rapid growth of the testis may predispose to torsion
Spontaneous detorsion occurs in about 10% of cases
questions.correctAnswer: A) It peaks in age 20-30 years
questions.explanation: Testicular torsion actually peaks in adolescence (approximately 12-16 years), not the 20-30 age range; rapid testicular growth and spontaneous detorsion in a minority of cases are recognized features.

questions.text: Is serum lactate a sensitive marker to rule out acute bowel ischemia?
options: True; lactate lacks adequate sensitivity, and a normal value does not exclude ischemia
False; a normal lactate reliably excludes bowel ischemia
True, but only in pediatric patients
False; lactate is always elevated in early ischemia
originalOptions: True; lactate lacks adequate sensitivity, and a normal value does not exclude ischemia
False; a normal lactate reliably excludes bowel ischemia
True, but only in pediatric patients
False; lactate is always elevated in early ischemia
questions.correctAnswer: A) True; lactate lacks adequate sensitivity, and a normal value does not exclude ischemia
questions.correctAnswerText: True; lactate lacks adequate sensitivity, and a normal value does not exclude ischemia
questions.explanation: Lactate may rise late in the course of mesenteric ischemia, so a normal or low value must not delay CT angiography when clinical suspicion is meaningful.

questions.text: Is the pain of acute mesenteric ischemia sometimes poorly relieved by analgesics?
options: True; the pain is classically out of proportion to exam findings and may remain poorly responsive to analgesics
False; mesenteric ischemia pain always resolves completely with standard analgesia
True, but only in chronic mesenteric ischemia
False; pain relief with analgesics confirms the diagnosis
originalOptions: True; the pain is classically out of proportion to exam findings and may remain poorly responsive to analgesics
False; mesenteric ischemia pain always resolves completely with standard analgesia
True, but only in chronic mesenteric ischemia
False; pain relief with analgesics confirms the diagnosis
questions.correctAnswer: A) True; the pain is classically out of proportion to exam findings and may remain poorly responsive to analgesics
questions.correctAnswerText: True; the pain is classically out of proportion to exam findings and may remain poorly responsive to analgesics
questions.explanation: Poor response to analgesia is a diagnostic clue (not a diagnostic test) in acute mesenteric ischemia, which classically causes severe pain disproportionate to physical exam findings; analgesia should still be given while arranging urgent CTA.

questions.text: How does the classic symptom triad of chronic mesenteric ischemia differ from acute mesenteric ischemia?
options: Chronic disease causes sudden severe pain; acute disease causes postprandial pain and weight loss
Chronic disease causes postprandial pain, food fear, and weight loss; acute disease causes sudden severe pain out of proportion to exam findings
Both present identically with sudden onset pain
originalOptions: Chronic disease causes sudden severe pain; acute disease causes postprandial pain and weight loss
Chronic disease causes postprandial pain, food fear, and weight loss; acute disease causes sudden severe pain out of proportion to exam findings
Both present identically with sudden onset pain
questions.correctAnswer: B) Chronic disease causes postprandial pain, food fear, and weight loss; acute disease causes sudden severe pain out of proportion to exam findings
questions.correctAnswerText: Chronic disease causes postprandial pain, food fear, and weight loss; acute disease causes sudden severe pain out of proportion to exam findings
questions.explanation: Chronic mesenteric ischemia reflects progressive atherosclerotic narrowing causing "intestinal angina" (postprandial pain, sitophobia, weight loss), whereas acute ischemia presents abruptly with severe pain disproportionate to initially unremarkable exam findings.

questions.text: What is the preferred initial imaging test when acute mesenteric ischemia is suspected?
questions.explanation: CT angiography is the preferred rapid diagnostic study for suspected acute mesenteric ischemia, allowing prompt visualization of mesenteric vasculature and bowel viability.

questions.text: Which of the following statements is WRONG?
options: Bowel strangulation/ischemia causes metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia
An elevated lactate supports mesenteric ischemia
originalOptions: Bowel strangulation/ischemia causes metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia
An elevated lactate supports mesenteric ischemia
questions.correctAnswer: A) Bowel strangulation/ischemia causes metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia
questions.correctAnswerText: Bowel strangulation/ischemia causes metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia
questions.explanation: Bowel strangulation classically produces lactic (metabolic) acidosis from tissue hypoperfusion, not alkalosis; hypokalemic, hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis is instead associated with vomiting/GI fluid losses, an independent mechanism.

questions.text: How do patients classically describe the pain of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm?
options: A dull, intermittent ache that improves with rest
The most severe/worst pain of their life — sudden, severe, tearing abdominal/flank/back pain
Mild colicky pain relieved by antacids
originalOptions: A dull, intermittent ache that improves with rest
The most severe/worst pain of their life — sudden, severe, tearing abdominal/flank/back pain
Mild colicky pain relieved by antacids
questions.correctAnswer: B) The most severe/worst pain of their life — sudden, severe, tearing abdominal/flank/back pain
questions.correctAnswerText: The most severe/worst pain of their life — sudden, severe, tearing abdominal/flank/back pain
questions.explanation: Ruptured AAA classically presents with sudden, excruciating, tearing pain often associated with hypotension and a pulsatile abdominal mass, reflecting acute hemorrhage into the retroperitoneum or peritoneal cavity.

questions.text: Which is the most important predictor of abdominal aortic aneurysm rupture?
questions.correctAnswer: D) Size (maximum diameter) of the aneurysm
questions.explanation: Aneurysm diameter is the single strongest predictor of rupture risk, with rapid expansion and symptomatic aneurysms also raising concern; smoking and uncontrolled hypertension are contributory but secondary risk factors.

allQuestions.text: What is the primary treatment goal in managing sinus tachycardia?
options: Identify and treat the underlying cause
originalOptions: Identify and treat the underlying cause
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Identify and treat the underlying cause
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Identify and treat the underlying cause
allQuestions.explanation: Sinus tachycardia is usually a physiologic response to an underlying stressor (pain, fever, hypovolemia, etc.); treating the cause resolves the tachycardia,whereas adenosine and cardioversion are for reentrant arrhythmias, not sinus tach.

allQuestions.text: After delivering a defibrillation shock to a patient in VF/pulseless VT, what is the immediate next step?
options: Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
originalOptions: Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Resume CPR immediately, starting with chest compressions
allQuestions.explanation: CPR must resume immediately after a shock without pausing to check pulse or rhythm, since even a successful shock rarely produces an immediately palpable pulse; rhythm is reassessed after the 2-minute CPR cycle.

allQuestions.text: In adult cardiac arrest, when is the first dose of epinephrine given, and how often is it repeated?
options: 1 mg IV/IO once, immediately after the first shock
1 mg IV/IO every 10 minutes throughout the arrest
2 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes starting immediately
1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
originalOptions: 1 mg IV/IO once, immediately after the first shock
1 mg IV/IO every 10 minutes throughout the arrest
2 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes starting immediately
1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: 1 mg IV/IO every 3-5 minutes, given as soon as possible in PEA/asystole or during the CPR cycle after the second shock in VF/pVT
allQuestions.explanation: Epinephrine dosing is time-interval based (every 3-5 minutes), not a fixed number of doses, and its first administration differs by rhythm: immediate in PEA/asystole, after the second shock in VF/pVT.

allQuestions.text: Which drug is used specifically to treat torsades de pointes during cardiac arrest management?
allQuestions.explanation: Magnesium sulfate directly stabilizes the myocardial membrane in torsades de pointes, unlike amiodarone/lidocaine which are used for refractory VF/pVT, or sodium bicarbonate which is reserved for hyperkalemia, TCA overdose, or severe acidosis.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is used for cardiac reperfusion in an ACS patient when timely PCI is unavailable?
options: Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
originalOptions: Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Fibrinolytic therapy, if the patient has an eligible STEMI and PCI is not available in time
allQuestions.explanation: Fibrinolytics achieve coronary reperfusion when timely PCI cannot be performed; epinephrine and atropine have no role in coronary reperfusion.

allQuestions.text: In the VF/pulseless VT algorithm, when are epinephrine and amiodarone typically administered relative to defibrillation?
options: Epinephrine after every shock; amiodarone after the first shock
Epinephrine every 10 minutes; amiodarone after the fifth shock
Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
Epinephrine only once at the start; amiodarone continuously infused
originalOptions: Epinephrine after every shock; amiodarone after the first shock
Epinephrine every 10 minutes; amiodarone after the fifth shock
Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
Epinephrine only once at the start; amiodarone continuously infused
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, given during the CPR cycle after the second shock; amiodarone (or lidocaine) for refractory VF/pVT typically after the third shock
allQuestions.explanation: The standard sequence gives epinephrine after the second shock and repeats it every 3-5 minutes; amiodarone/lidocaine are added for shock-refractory VF/pVT after the third shock, without ever replacing CPR or defibrillation.

allQuestions.text: A 55-year-old male has stroke symptoms, and CT shows multilobar infarction (more than one-third of the cerebral hemisphere). What therapy is contraindicated?
allQuestions.explanation: A large established infarct substantially increases the risk of hemorrhagic transformation with thrombolysis; current decisions also weigh time window, disabling deficit, and modern imaging criteria rather than this legacy size cutoff alone.

allQuestions.text: A 79-year-old patient in supraventricular tachycardia has a blood pressure of 80/50 and complains of chest discomfort with near-syncope. What is the next appropriate step?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypotension and chest discomfort attributable to the tachyarrhythmia define instability, requiring immediate synchronized cardioversion; carotid massage risks complications in elderly patients, and amiodarone/lidocaine are not first-line for unstable SVT.

allQuestions.text: _______ access is preferred in cardiac arrest due to easy access and no interruption in CPR.
allQuestions.explanation: Peripheral IV access can be obtained without interrupting chest compressions and carries fewer complications than central lines, making it the preferred first-line route during arrest.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are bradycardic rhythms except:
allQuestions.explanation: Atrial fibrillation is typically associated with an irregular, often rapid ventricular response, not bradycardia, unlike the listed AV blocks which characteristically slow ventricular rate.

allQuestions.text: Choose the correct sequence of electrical activity in the heart for normal sinus rhythm.
options: SA node, Purkinje fibers, AV node, Bundle of His
Purkinje fibers, Bundle of His, AV node, SA node
SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
AV node, SA node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
originalOptions: SA node, Purkinje fibers, AV node, Bundle of His
Purkinje fibers, Bundle of His, AV node, SA node
SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
AV node, SA node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: SA node, AV node, Bundle of His, Purkinje fibers
allQuestions.explanation: The normal conduction pathway originates in the SA node, passes through the AV node, then the Bundle of His, and finally the Purkinje fibers to depolarize the ventricles.

allQuestions.text: In children and infants, when should 2 minutes of CPR be given before activating EMS in a single-rescuer scenario?
options: Unresponsive victim with pulse and breathing
originalOptions: Unresponsive victim with pulse and breathing
allQuestions.explanation: For an unwitnessed pediatric collapse, a lone rescuer should perform about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to activate EMS/get an AED, since the initial cause is often respiratory rather than a witnessed cardiac event.

allQuestions.text: In CPR, what is the maximum time a rescuer should take to check for a pulse?
allQuestions.explanation: If a definite pulse is not felt within 10 seconds, the rescuer should begin or resume CPR without further delay to avoid prolonging a no-flow state.

allQuestions.text: Most cases of pediatric cardiac arrest begin with which underlying process?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Respiratory distress/failure or shock (asphyxial arrest)
allQuestions.explanation: Unlike adults, most pediatric arrests are asphyxial, progressing from respiratory failure or shock rather than a primary shockable arrhythmia — this is why early ventilation is emphasized in pediatric resuscitation.

allQuestions.text: What best describes the traditional stroke-care time benchmarks of ED evaluation within 10 minutes, neurologic evaluation within 25 minutes, and head CT read within 45 minutes of arrival?
options: These are current mandatory legal requirements in all hospitals
These are outdated absolute rules that should never be exceeded
These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
These times apply only to hemorrhagic stroke
originalOptions: These are current mandatory legal requirements in all hospitals
These are outdated absolute rules that should never be exceeded
These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
These times apply only to hemorrhagic stroke
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: These are legacy process targets; current care still requires immediate evaluation and rapid imaging without avoidable delay, per local stroke protocol
allQuestions.explanation: These specific minute-benchmarks are legacy process targets rather than fixed universal rules; the underlying principle of minimizing delay to imaging and treatment remains current.

allQuestions.text: When should out-of-hospital resuscitation efforts be terminated in adults?
options: After exactly 20 minutes of CPR regardless of rhythm
Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
originalOptions: After exactly 20 minutes of CPR regardless of rhythm
Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Based on a validated termination-of-resuscitation rule (arrest not witnessed by EMS, no shock delivered, no ROSC), combined with clinical judgment
allQuestions.explanation: Termination decisions rely on validated criteria and clinical/legal judgment rather than an arbitrary elapsed time; in-hospital decisions remain individualized.

allQuestions.text: Select the proper pairing regarding chest compressions for an adult.
options: 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
originalOptions: 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: 100 to 120 compressions/minute; 2 to 2.4 inches (5-6 cm) deep
allQuestions.explanation: High-quality adult CPR requires a compression rate of 100-120/min and a depth of 5-6 cm, avoiding both underventilation of blood flow and excessive depth that risks injury.

allQuestions.text: Symptomatic bradycardia (HR 32, hypotension, altered mental status): what is the first-line medication?
allQuestions.explanation: Atropine is the first-line drug for symptomatic bradycardia; dopamine or epinephrine infusions and transcutaneous pacing are reserved as next-line options if atropine fails, not co-first-line agents.

allQuestions.text: In the treatment of a stable tachyarrhythmia, how many CPR cycles must elapse before reassessing the rhythm?
options: CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
originalOptions: CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: CPR cycles are not the relevant measure — reassessment depends on the patient's response to treatment (vagal maneuvers, adenosine, or cardioversion), not a fixed number of CPR cycles
allQuestions.explanation: The tachycardia-with-a-pulse algorithm is response-driven, not cycle-counted like the pulseless arrest algorithm; "5 CPR cycles" is a pulseless-arrest concept misapplied here.

allQuestions.text: The 6 steps in the Adult Chain of Survival include all of the following except:
allQuestions.explanation: The Chain of Survival emphasizes early recognition/CPR, rapid defibrillation, and integrated post-arrest care; routine cardiovascular medications are not one of its defined links.
allQuestions.note: The Adult Chain of Survival (AHA, out-of-hospital version) has 6 links: 1. Recognition of cardiac arrest and activation of emergency response . 2. Early, high-quality CPR . 3. Rapid defibrillation . 4. Advanced resuscitation (ACLS) . 5. Post-cardiac arrest care . 6. Recovery .

allQuestions.text: Which elements are included in the ACLS Survey?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Airway, Breathing, Circulation, Differential diagnosis
allQuestions.explanation: The ACLS Survey (as opposed to the BLS Survey) systematically assesses Airway, Breathing, Circulation, and Differential diagnosis to identify and treat reversible causes.

allQuestions.text: What term describes an organized electrical rhythm with no palpable pulse, and how is it treated?
options: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
Ventricular fibrillation; treat with immediate defibrillation
Pulseless VT; treat with synchronized cardioversion
originalOptions: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
Ventricular fibrillation; treat with immediate defibrillation
Pulseless VT; treat with synchronized cardioversion
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA); treat with high-quality CPR, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and correction of reversible causes (do not shock)
allQuestions.explanation: PEA is defined by an organized rhythm without a detectable pulse; it is not shockable, so treatment centers on CPR, epinephrine, and correcting the underlying Hs and Ts

allQuestions.text: The normal sinus rhythm of the heart starts in the:
allQuestions.explanation: The SA node is the heart's natural pacemaker, initiating the electrical impulse that spreads through the atria to the AV node.

allQuestions.text: The primary focus of treating cardiac arrest is:
options: Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
originalOptions: Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Both effective CPR and early defibrillation
allQuestions.explanation: High-quality CPR and early defibrillation are the two interventions most strongly linked to survival in cardiac arrest, more so than drug administration.

allQuestions.text: A 3-year-old child begins breathing at 18 breaths/min and has a pulse of 50/min. What should you do next?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Begin CPR with chest compressions
allQuestions.explanation: CPR should be initiated in pediatric patients whose pulse is ≤60/min despite adequate oxygenation and ventilation, since this reflects inadequate perfusion.

allQuestions.text: What age is considered an infant for BLS purposes?
allQuestions.explanation: BLS classifications define an infant as under one year of age, a child as 1 year to puberty, and adolescents and older as the adult category.

allQuestions.text: What does the QRS complex on an ECG represent?
allQuestions.explanation: The QRS complex reflects ventricular depolarization leading to contraction; the T wave, not the QRS, represents ventricular repolarization.

allQuestions.text: What factor is critical to assess in any emergency situation before approaching the patient?
allQuestions.explanation: Scene safety must always be confirmed first so the rescuer does not become a second casualty, before any patient-specific assessment is made.

allQuestions.text: What is the first step in the assessment of an individual found "down"?
options: Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
originalOptions: Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Check to see if they are conscious or unconscious
allQuestions.explanation: Establishing responsiveness is the first assessment step, as it determines whether the emergency response/resuscitation sequence should be activated.

allQuestions.text: What is the recommended method to monitor breathing/ventilation during ACLS care?
Where should you attempt to perform a pulse check in an adult?
allQuestions.explanation: The carotid artery is the standard site for adult pulse checks due to its accessibility and reliability during low-flow states.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is first-line treatment for ACS?
allQuestions.explanation: Aspirin provides mortality benefit in acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and is given to essentially all eligible patients, whereas morphine and nitroglycerin are selective symptom therapies rather than universal first-line treatment.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT an example of an advanced airway?
allQuestions.explanation: An OPA is a basic airway adjunct, unlike the esophageal-tracheal tube, laryngeal mask airway, and Combitube, which are all advanced airway devices.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is true regarding BLS?
options: It has little impact on survival
It should be mastered prior to ACLS
originalOptions: It has little impact on survival
It should be mastered prior to ACLS
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) It should be mastered prior to ACLS
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It should be mastered prior to ACLS
allQuestions.explanation: ACLS providers are presumed to have already mastered BLS skills, since high-quality CPR remains foundational to resuscitation outcomes.

allQuestions.text: Which sequence best represents the adult Chain of Survival?
options: Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, provide ventilations, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, wait for advanced care, recovery
originalOptions: Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, provide ventilations, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, defibrillate, recovery
Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, wait for advanced care, recovery
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Check responsiveness, call EMS/AED, begin chest compressions, provide early defibrillation, recovery
allQuestions.explanation: The Chain of Survival emphasizes early CPR (chest compressions) and early defibrillation as the key steps between activation of emergency response and recovery.

allQuestions.text: While one rescuer is performing CPR on an infant, a second rescuer arrives. What should happen next?
options: The second rescuer takes over compressions alone while the first rescuer leaves
The second rescuer waits until the first rescuer is exhausted
The second rescuer immediately applies AED pads without confirming EMS activation
The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
originalOptions: The second rescuer takes over compressions alone while the first rescuer leaves
The second rescuer waits until the first rescuer is exhausted
The second rescuer immediately applies AED pads without confirming EMS activation
The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The second rescuer activates the emergency response system/retrieves the AED if not already done, then assists with two-rescuer CPR
allQuestions.explanation: Two-rescuer infant CPR uses coordinated roles — one ensures EMS/AED activation while the other continues compressions — rather than one rescuer working alone or waiting

allQuestions.text: During adult CPR with an advanced airway in place, what ventilation rate should be used?
options: One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
originalOptions: One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: One breath every 6 seconds with continuous chest compressions
allQuestions.explanation: Once an advanced airway is placed, compressions are continuous and ventilations are delivered asynchronously at one breath every 6 seconds (10/min), avoiding pauses in compressions.

allQuestions.text: You are alone with an unresponsive 3-year-old child who is not breathing and appears cyanotic. What should you do first?
options: Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
Leave immediately to activate EMS and get an AED
Give rescue breaths only for 2 minutes
Place the child in the recovery position
originalOptions: Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
Leave immediately to activate EMS and get an AED
Give rescue breaths only for 2 minutes
Place the child in the recovery position
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Give about 2 minutes of CPR, then activate EMS and get an AED
allQuestions.explanation: For an unwitnessed pediatric arrest with a lone rescuer, 2 minutes of CPR should be performed before leaving the child to activate EMS/retrieve an AED, since pediatric arrests are often asphyxial and respond to early ventilation/compressions.

allQuestions.text: You are transporting an individual who goes into cardiac arrest during transport. IV access is unsuccessful. What is the next step?
options: Administer all medications through the ET tube
originalOptions: Administer all medications through the ET tube
allQuestions.explanation: IO access can be established rapidly and is the preferred next route for drug delivery when IV access fails, since ET tube drug absorption is unreliable and central lines interrupt CPR.

allQuestions.text: CPR is initiated and the patient's pulse returns, but he is not breathing normally. What ventilation rate should be used?
options: 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
originalOptions: 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: 10 breaths per minute (1 breath every 6 seconds), with visible chest rise
allQuestions.explanation: For an adult with a pulse who is not breathing normally, rescue breathing is given at one breath every 6 seconds (10/min) with visible chest rise, per current AHA guidance.

allQuestions.text: What is the single-rescuer adult chest compression-to-ventilation ratio before placement of an advanced airway?
options: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway
originalOptions: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: 30 compressions to 2 breaths, before placement of an advanced airway
allQuestions.explanation: Without an advanced airway, adult CPR uses a 30:2 compression-to-ventilation ratio; once an advanced airway is placed, ventilation becomes continuous at one breath every 6 seconds. ###d In two-rescuer adult CPR, after an advanced airway is placed, what is the compression-to-ventilation approach? A) Continuous compressions at 100-120/min with 1 breath every 6 seconds B) 30:2 C) 15:2 D) 30:1 Correct Answer: A) Continuous compressions at 100-120/min with 1 breath every 6 seconds Explanation: After advanced airway placement, compressions become continuous (not paused for breaths) while ventilations are delivered asynchronously every 6 seconds.

allQuestions.text: During high-quality CPR, what ETCO2 range indicates adequate chest compressions?
allQuestions.explanation: An ETCO2 of at least 10-20 mmHg during CPR reflects adequate compressions and perfusion; persistently low ETCO2 suggests poor CPR quality, while a sudden rise to ≥40 mmHg suggests ROSC.

allQuestions.text: According to current guidelines, what is the pediatric chest compression-to-ventilation ratio for single-rescuer versus two-rescuer CPR (without an advanced airway)?
options: 15:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
30:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
originalOptions: 15:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
30:2 for all scenarios regardless of rescuer number
allQuestions.explanation: Pediatric CPR uses 30:2 for a lone rescuer (matching adult ratio) but shifts to 15:2 when a second rescuer is present to allow more frequent ventilation for the child.

allQuestions.text: What are the possible effects of hyperventilation during CPR?
options: Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
Decreased venous return to the heart
originalOptions: Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
Decreased venous return to the heart
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Increased intrathoracic pressure and decreased venous return to the heart (both)
allQuestions.explanation: Excessive ventilation raises intrathoracic pressure, which impedes venous return to the heart and reduces cardiac output generated by compressions.

allQuestions.text: Why are ventilations given to a pediatric arrest victim before seeking assistance in a single-rescuer scenario?
options: Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
AED use is contraindicated in pediatrics
originalOptions: Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
AED use is contraindicated in pediatrics
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Most pediatric cardiac arrests are due to respiratory arrest
allQuestions.explanation: Since pediatric arrests are predominantly asphyxial, restoring oxygenation/ventilation early can be lifesaving and may prevent progression to full cardiac arrest

allQuestions.text: Pulseless electrical activity (PEA) includes any pulseless rhythm EXCEPT which of the following?
options: Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
originalOptions: Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Ventricular fibrillation, pulseless VT, and true asystole
allQuestions.explanation: PEA is defined as any organized pulseless rhythm; VF, pulseless VT, and true asystole are managed as separate distinct categories in the cardiac arrest algorithm and are excluded from the PEA definition.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following can present as pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
options: Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
originalOptions: Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Any organized rhythm without a pulse (e.g., sinus rhythm, sinus bradycardia, idioventricular, or junctional rhythm)
allQuestions.explanation: PEA encompasses any organized electrical activity on the monitor that lacks a detectable pulse, while VF, pulseless VT, and asystole are treated as separate rhythm categories.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of pulseless electrical activity (PEA)?
allQuestions.explanation: PEA causes follow the 5H/5T mnemonic (Hypoxia, Hypovolemia, Hydrogen ion/acidosis, Hypo/Hyperkalemia, Hypothermia, Tension pneumothorax, Tamponade, Toxins, Thrombosis, Trauma); hyperventilation is not one of these reversible causes.

allQuestions.text: Which medication can be used to treat hypotension during the post-cardiac arrest phase?
allQuestions.explanation: Dopamine is a vasopressor/inotrope used to support blood pressure in the post-arrest period; amiodarone treats arrhythmias, and milrinone is not typically used for post-arrest hypotension.

allQuestions.text: After activating EMS and sending someone for an AED, what is the correct action for one-rescuer BLS of an unresponsive individual with no pulse?
allQuestions.explanation: Once help has been activated, the lone rescuer should immediately begin chest compressions, since compressions take priority in adult CPR sequencing.

allQuestions.text: In which of the following situations should the AED NOT be applied without first modifying the patient or environment?
options: Victim with an implanted pacemaker (pad placement adjusted)
Victim with a transdermal medication patch (patch removed first)
Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
originalOptions: Victim with an implanted pacemaker (pad placement adjusted)
Victim with a transdermal medication patch (patch removed first)
Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Victim lying partially in water (should be moved to a dry area first)
allQuestions.explanation: Water on the chest can short-circuit or reduce shock delivery, so the victim must be moved to a dry area and dried before AED use; pacemakers and patches only require adjusted pad placement or removal, not avoidance of the AED.

allQuestions.text: A patient with a pulse has unstable monomorphic ventricular tachycardia with hypotension and altered mental status. What is the indicated treatment?
allQuestions.explanation: Unstable VT with a pulse requires immediate synchronized cardioversion; amiodarone is an adjunct for stable or refractory VT, not the first action in instability.

allQuestions.text: At what age is it preferable to use pediatric AED pads instead of adult pads?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Less than 8 years of age
allQuestions.explanation: Pediatric AED pads/attenuated energy settings are preferred for children under 8 years old to deliver an age-appropriate energy dose; adult pads are used for older children and adults.

allQuestions.text: How much energy is delivered for an adult shock with a monophasic defibrillator?
allQuestions.explanation: Monophasic defibrillators deliver a fixed 360 J for all adult shocks, unlike biphasic devices which use 120-200 J per manufacturer recommendation.

allQuestions.text: A patient in pulseless VT receives CPR/defibrillation cycles and remains pulseless, now with an organized SVT-like rhythm on the monitor. What is the next step?
options: Treat as pulseless electrical activity (PEA): resume high-quality CPR, give epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and treat reversible causes; do not shock unless VF/pulseless VT recurs
Continue treating as pulseless VT with another shock
Give adenosine to convert the SVT-like rhythm
Shock the new rhythm since it originated from pulseless VT
originalOptions: Treat as pulseless electrical activity (PEA): resume high-quality CPR, give epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and treat reversible causes; do not shock unless VF/pulseless VT recurs
Continue treating as pulseless VT with another shock
Give adenosine to convert the SVT-like rhythm
Shock the new rhythm since it originated from pulseless VT
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Treat as pulseless electrical activity (PEA): resume high-quality CPR, give epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and treat reversible causes; do not shock unless VF/pulseless VT recurs
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Treat as pulseless electrical activity (PEA): resume high-quality CPR, give epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and treat reversible causes; do not shock unless VF/pulseless VT recurs
allQuestions.explanation: Treatment is dictated by the current pulseless rhythm, not the preceding one; an organized rhythm without a pulse is PEA and should not be shocked unless VF/pulseless VT recurs.

allQuestions.text: What are the criteria for applying an AED to a collapsed patient?
options: The patient is unresponsive but has a strong pulse
The patient is breathing normally but confused
The patient is responsive with chest pain
The patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no definite pulse
originalOptions: The patient is unresponsive but has a strong pulse
The patient is breathing normally but confused
The patient is responsive with chest pain
The patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no definite pulse
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no definite pulse
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The patient is unresponsive, not breathing normally, and has no definite pulse
allQuestions.explanation: An AED should be applied as soon as available to a patient meeting all three criteria — unresponsive, abnormal/absent breathing, and no definite pulse — with minimal interruption of CPR to attach it.

allQuestions.text: What is the recommended defibrillation energy for monophasic versus biphasic defibrillators?
options: Monophasic: 200 J for all shocks; Biphasic: 360 J fixed
Monophasic: 360 J for all shocks; Biphasic: 120-200 J per manufacturer recommendation (or maximum available dose if unknown)
Both monophasic and biphasic use 150 J fixed
originalOptions: Monophasic: 200 J for all shocks; Biphasic: 360 J fixed
Monophasic: 360 J for all shocks; Biphasic: 120-200 J per manufacturer recommendation (or maximum available dose if unknown)
Both monophasic and biphasic use 150 J fixed
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Monophasic: 360 J for all shocks; Biphasic: 120-200 J per manufacturer recommendation (or maximum available dose if unknown)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Monophasic: 360 J for all shocks; Biphasic: 120-200 J per manufacturer recommendation (or maximum available dose if unknown)
allQuestions.explanation: Monophasic defibrillators use a fixed 360 J dose, while biphasic devices deliver lower energy (120-200 J) per manufacturer guidance, defaulting to maximum available energy if unspecified.

allQuestions.text: The AED indicates "Shock." What is the next step?
options: Deliver two additional minutes of CPR before delivering the shock
Ventilate while the shock is delivered
Assume error and do not deliver the shock
Clear the person and deliver the shock
originalOptions: Deliver two additional minutes of CPR before delivering the shock
Ventilate while the shock is delivered
Assume error and do not deliver the shock
Clear the person and deliver the shock
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Clear the person and deliver the shock
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Clear the person and deliver the shock
allQuestions.explanation: Once the AED advises a shock, the rescuer should ensure everyone is clear of the patient and deliver it promptly, without delaying for additional CPR or assuming device error.

allQuestions.text: Which listed medication is NOT used in the adult algorithm for persistent ventricular fibrillation or pulseless ventricular tachycardia?
allQuestions.explanation: Persistent VF/pulseless VT management relies on defibrillation, high-quality CPR, epinephrine, and amiodarone/lidocaine; atropine has no role in shockable pulseless arrest.

allQuestions.text: What are the proper steps for operating an AED?
options: Power on the AED, attach electrode pads, analyze the rhythm, and shock the person
Power on the AED, attach electrode pads, shock the person, and analyze the rhythm
Power on the AED, analyze the rhythm, attach electrode pads, and shock the person
Power on the AED, shock the person, attach electrode pads, and analyze the rhythm
originalOptions: Power on the AED, attach electrode pads, analyze the rhythm, and shock the person
Power on the AED, attach electrode pads, shock the person, and analyze the rhythm
Power on the AED, analyze the rhythm, attach electrode pads, and shock the person
Power on the AED, shock the person, attach electrode pads, and analyze the rhythm
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Power on the AED, attach electrode pads, analyze the rhythm, and shock the person
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Power on the AED, attach electrode pads, analyze the rhythm, and shock the person
allQuestions.explanation: The AED must be powered on and pads attached before it can analyze the rhythm; a shock is only delivered after rhythm analysis confirms a shockable rhythm.

allQuestions.text: How is refractory ventricular fibrillation managed in the adult cardiac arrest algorithm?
options: Stop CPR and give epinephrine alone
Give atropine as the primary antiarrhythmic
Continue high-quality CPR with repeated defibrillation, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and amiodarone or lidocaine (typically after the third shock), while treating reversible causes
originalOptions: Stop CPR and give epinephrine alone
Give atropine as the primary antiarrhythmic
Continue high-quality CPR with repeated defibrillation, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and amiodarone or lidocaine (typically after the third shock), while treating reversible causes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Continue high-quality CPR with repeated defibrillation, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and amiodarone or lidocaine (typically after the third shock), while treating reversible causes
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Continue high-quality CPR with repeated defibrillation, epinephrine every 3-5 minutes, and amiodarone or lidocaine (typically after the third shock), while treating reversible causes
allQuestions.explanation: Refractory VF is managed by continuing CPR and defibrillation with epinephrine and adding amiodarone or lidocaine (usually after the third shock), while actively searching for reversible causes.

allQuestions.text: What does AED stand for?
allQuestions.explanation: AED stands for Automated External Defibrillator, a device that analyzes cardiac rhythm and delivers a shock if a shockable rhythm is detected.

allQuestions.text: What is the first step after detecting a shockable rhythm on the defibrillator?
options: Deliver shock and immediately resume CPR
originalOptions: Deliver shock and immediately resume CPR
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Deliver shock and immediately resume CPR
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Deliver shock and immediately resume CPR
allQuestions.explanation: Once a shockable rhythm is confirmed, the shock should be delivered promptly and CPR resumed immediately afterward, without pausing for a pulse check or drug administration first.

allQuestions.text: When should rhythm be checked after using an AED?
options: After one 2-minute CPR cycle (or whenever the AED prompts a rhythm analysis)
originalOptions: After one 2-minute CPR cycle (or whenever the AED prompts a rhythm analysis)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) After one 2-minute CPR cycle (or whenever the AED prompts a rhythm analysis)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: After one 2-minute CPR cycle (or whenever the AED prompts a rhythm analysis)
allQuestions.explanation: CPR resumes immediately after a shock and continues for a full 2-minute cycle before the rhythm is reassessed, avoiding an immediate pulse/rhythm pause.

allQuestions.text: Where are standard anterolateral AED pads placed?
options: Right upper chest (below the right clavicle) and left lower/lateral chest (below the left armpit)
Both pads on the anterior chest, side by side
Right lower chest and left upper chest
Directly over the sternum, one above the other
originalOptions: Right upper chest (below the right clavicle) and left lower/lateral chest (below the left armpit)
Both pads on the anterior chest, side by side
Right lower chest and left upper chest
Directly over the sternum, one above the other
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Right upper chest (below the right clavicle) and left lower/lateral chest (below the left armpit)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Right upper chest (below the right clavicle) and left lower/lateral chest (below the left armpit)
allQuestions.explanation: The anterolateral placement positions one pad below the right clavicle and the other on the left lateral chest below the armpit, maximizing current flow through the heart.

allQuestions.text: An unresponsive patient regains a pulse after defibrillation for ventricular fibrillation, and the post-shock ECG shows third-degree AV block with a slow ventricular rate. What is the next most appropriate step in management?
allQuestions.explanation: With a pulse present, symptomatic complete heart block is treated with transcutaneous pacing (± dopamine/epinephrine infusion) rather than defibrillation or chest compressions, which are reserved for pulseless rhythms.
allQuestions.note: Without a pulse, this is PEA: resume CPR and give epinephrine; routine pacing during established arrest is not recommended.

allQuestions.text: The recovered ECG shows P waves marching out independently from QRS complexes at a faster rate than the ventricular rate, with no fixed relationship between P and QRS. What is the diagnosis? [img: ERArrhythmia1.png ]
options: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
originalOptions: Mobitz type II second-degree AV block
allQuestions.explanation: Complete AV dissociation — P waves and QRS complexes occurring independently with the atrial rate faster than the ventricular escape rate — defines third-degree AV block, unlike Mobitz I/II where some P waves still conduct.

allQuestions.text: Which statement correctly differentiates Mobitz type I from Mobitz type II second-degree AV block?
options: Mobitz I has a constant PR interval with sudden dropped beats; Mobitz II shows progressive PR prolongation
Both types show progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Mobitz II is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS and low risk of complete block

Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
originalOptions: Mobitz I has a constant PR interval with sudden dropped beats; Mobitz II shows progressive PR prolongation
Both types show progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Mobitz II is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS and low risk of complete block

Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Mobitz I shows progressive PR prolongation until a P wave is not conducted and is usually AV-nodal with a narrow QRS; Mobitz II has constant PR intervals with sudden nonconducted beats and is usually infranodal with a wide QRS
allQuestions.explanation: Mobitz I reflects reversible AV-nodal delay with progressive PR lengthening before a dropped beat; Mobitz II is an infranodal block with fixed PR intervals and a higher risk of progressing to complete heart block.

allQuestions.text: A 12-lead ECG shows a constant PR interval of 240 ms with every P wave followed by a QRS complex. What is the diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A fixed PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction (no dropped beats) defines first-degree AV block, a partial delay rather than an interruption of conduction.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia2.png ] The ECG shows constant PR intervals with intermittent nonconducted P waves in a patient with an acute anterior wall MI. What is the most appropriate next step?
options: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
originalOptions: Give atropine only, with no further action
Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Ensure urgent temporary pacing capability and cardiology evaluation
allQuestions.explanation: Mobitz II or high-grade AV block complicating anterior MI reflects extensive infranodal conduction system damage and can progress abruptly to complete block/asystole, so urgent pacing readiness and cardiology evaluation are required rather than observation or AV-nodal blocking drugs.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia3.png ] An asymptomatic 29-year-old has first-degree AV block on this ECG with no other conduction disease. What is the best next step?
options: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
originalOptions: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: No acute treatment; review medications and confirm the cause
allQuestions.explanation: Isolated, asymptomatic first-degree AV block requires no acute intervention beyond identifying reversible causes (e.g., AV-nodal blocking drugs); cardioversion and defibrillation are irrelevant since this is not a tachyarrhythma

allQuestions.text: What are the defining ECG features of complete (third-degree) AV block?
options: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
originalOptions: Progressive PR prolongation before a dropped beat
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
Fixed PR interval with intermittent nonconducted P waves
Constant PR interval >200 ms with 1:1 conduction
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes, with the atrial rate exceeding the ventricular escape rate
allQuestions.explanation: In third-degree block, P waves and QRS complexes occur completely independently (AV dissociation), with the atrial rate faster than the escape ventricular rate; the escape QRS is narrow if junctional, wide if ventricular/infranodal.

allQuestions.text: What ECG finding is diagnostic of complete (third-degree) heart block?
options: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats
Short PR interval with a delta wave
Irregularly irregular rhythm without P waves
Complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes
originalOptions: Fixed PR interval with dropped beats

allQuestions.explanation: The hallmark of complete heart block is total dissociation of atrial and ventricular activity — P waves and QRS complexes occur independently at their own rates.

allQuestions.text: A patient develops Mobitz II AV block complicating an acute anterior wall MI. When is a permanent pacemaker indicated?
options: Only if the patient develops asystole
Never; anterior MI-related block always resolves
If the infranodal block persists despite treatment of reversible causes, since anterior MI-related block reflects extensive septal damage and carries a high risk of progression

Never; anterior MI-related block always resolves

allQuestions.explanation: Anterior MI causing Mobitz II/high-grade block indicates extensive septal/infranodal damage with a high risk of sudden complete block or asystole; if it persists after reversible causes are addressed, permanent pacing is indicated.

allQuestions.text: A patient has atrial fibrillation of unknown duration and is hemodynamically stable. What anticoagulation strategy should precede elective cardioversion?
options: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
No anticoagulation needed if cardioversion restores sinus rhythm
Anticoagulation is only needed after cardioversion, not before

allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Therapeutic anticoagulation for at least 3 weeks before and 4 weeks after cardioversion, or a TEE-guided strategy with peri- and post-procedural anticoagulation
allQuestions.explanation: For AF ≥48 hours or of unknown duration, guidelines require ≥3 weeks anticoagulation before and ≥4 weeks after elective cardioversion (or TEE exclusion of thrombus with periprocedural anticoagulation), because stroke risk depends on atrial stasis duration, not on restoration of sinus rhythm.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia4.png] A hemodynamically stable patient has atrial flutter with a ventricular rate around 130/min and no heart-failure symptoms. What is the best initial treatment?
options: A beta-blocker for ventricular rate control

allQuestions.text: Which arrhythmia is most commonly associated with thyrotoxicosis?
allQuestions.explanation: Thyrotoxicosis sensitizes atrial myocardium and is a classic reversible cause of atrial fibrillation; thyroid function should be checked in all new-onset AF.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] A patient has had palpitations for 1 week due to atrial fibrillation, with no syncope, heart failure, or chest pain. She is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step?
allQuestions.explanation: In stable AF with preserved LVEF, IV diltiazem provides acute ventricular rate control; cardioversion is not first-line without addressing anticoagulation given the AF duration is ≥48 hours, and defibrillation is inappropriate for a non-shockable rhythm with a pulse.

allQuestions.text: Which finding alone is NOT considered an ACLS sign of hemodynamic instability in a patient with atrial flutter?
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) A high ventricular rate alone
allQuestions.explanation: ACLS instability criteria require hypotension, altered mental status, shock, ischemic chest pain, or acute heart failure attributable to the arrhythmia; a fast rate by itself, without these findings, does not define instability.

allQuestions.text: In a patient with atrial fibrillation, which factor determines whether rate control or rhythm control is prioritized, and how should ventricular rate be managed if AF is hemodynamically stable?
options: If AF causes instability, perform immediate synchronized cardioversion; if stable, choose rate or rhythm control based on symptoms/comorbidities, using a beta-blocker as an acute rate-control option (diltiazem/verapamil reserved for LVEF >40%)
All stable AF patients require immediate cardioversion regardless of duration
Diltiazem is preferred over beta-blockers regardless of ejection fraction
Digoxin is always first-line for rate control

allQuestions.text: A hemodynamically stable patient with atrial fibrillation has an LVEF of 30%. Which agent should be avoided for ventricular rate control?
allQuestions.explanation: Non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers have negative inotropic effects and should be avoided when LVEF is below 40%; beta-blockers (if compensated), digoxin, or amiodarone in decompensated states are preferred alternatives.

allQuestions.text: A patient with Wolff-Parkinson-White syndrome presents in pre-excited atrial fibrillation. Which class of drugs must be avoided?
options: Class Ia antiarrhythmics such as procainamide
Isolated AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, beta-blockers, diltiazem/verapamil, digoxin)
Class III antiarrhythmics such as ibutilide

allQuestions.text: What is the primary indication for emergency electrical cardioversion in atrial fibrillation?
options: AF diagnosed incidentally on a routine ECG
AF lasting less than 12 hours regardless of symptoms
Recurrent paroxysmal AF with prior successful rate control
AF causing hemodynamic instability (hypotension, shock, pulmonary edema, or ongoing ischemia)

allQuestions.explanation: Emergency synchronized cardioversion is reserved for AF causing hemodynamic compromise; stable AF is managed with rate/rhythm-control strategies and appropriately timed anticoagulation.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] What rhythm is shown on this 12-lead ECG?
allQuestions.explanation: The tracing shows an irregularly irregular ventricular rhythm without discrete P waves, replaced by fine fibrillatory baseline oscillations — diagnostic of atrial fibrillation.

allQuestions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a heart rate of 32/min and a palpable pulse. Which of the following are acceptable therapeutic options if the initial drug is ineffective?
options: Atropine, followed by transcutaneous pacing and/or dopamine or epinephrine infusion
Immediate chest compressions regardless of pulse
Observation only, since bradycardia is never treated pharmacologically

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia5.png] An adult patient has symptomatic bradycardia with a pulse and poor perfusion. What is the correct approach to management?
options: Chest compressions, invasive airway, transcutaneous pacing

allQuestions.text: What defines sinus arrest, and how does its ECG pause differ from a sinoatrial exit block?

allQuestions.text: What is the first-line medication to treat symptomatic bradycardia?
allQuestions.explanation: Atropine is the first drug given in the adult symptomatic bradycardia algorithm because it reverses excessive vagal tone at the SA/AV node; beta-blockers and calcium channel blockers would worsen bradycardia.

allQuestions.text: A patient has symptomatic bradycardia with cardiopulmonary compromise. What is the correct atropine dosing and next step if ineffective?
options: Atropine 5 mg IV bolus, single dose

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is an EXTRINSIC (reversible) cause of bradycardia rather than intrinsic SA-node disease?

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a pathological, intrinsic cause of bradycardia rather than a normal physiological variant?
options: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child
originalOptions: High resting vagal tone in a trained athlete
Respiratory sinus arrhythmia in a healthy child
allQuestions.explanation: Sick sinus syndrome reflects intrinsic structural SA-node disease (typically idiopathic fibrosis), unlike athletic bradycardia, sleep-related bradycardia, or respiratory sinus arrhythmia, which are normal physiological findings.

allQuestions.text: How is sinus arrhythmia defined, and what does a non-phasic pattern suggest in the context of sick sinus syndrome?

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia6.png] A 55-year-old asthmatic patient presents with palpitations. and she is hemodynamically stable. What is the best next step for management?
allQuestions.explanation: In stable AF, rate control is first-line; diltiazem is preferred over a beta-blocker in this asthmatic patient to avoid bronchospasm, while adenosine and atropine have no role in AF.

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia19.png] A 73-year-old ICU patient becomes unresponsive with a tachyarrhythmia on ECG and a blood pressure of 70/40. What is the best next step for management?
allQuestions.explanation: A tachyarrhythmia causing severe hypotension and unresponsiveness is unstable; immediate synchronized cardioversion is indicated rather than pharmacologic rate/rhythm control

allQuestions.text: [img: ERArrhythmia7.png] A patient becomes unresponsive and the ECG shows ventricular fibrillation. What is the immediate next step?
options: Immediate unsynchronized defibrillation with high-quality CPR
