allQuestions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologycleftlowerlobecollapse.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Triangular density behind the heart. The left hilum is inferiorly displaced. Volume loss in the left hemithorax. Pneumothorax is lucent, effusion shows a meniscus, and consolidation preserves lobar volume.

allQuestions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologyctensionpneumothorax.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Mobile chest x-ray of an intubated patient with a large right-sided pneumothorax. The right hemithorax is hyper-expanded, the right ribs are splayed, the diaphragm is flattened, there is leftward shift of the mediastinum and the right lung is collapsed. Both lungs show signs of consolidation and this prevents further collapse of the right lung.

allQuestions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologycsarcoidosis.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: Bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy. No lung infiltrations are shown. No fibrosis. The plain film demonstrates stage 1 sarcoidosis (i.e. bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy).

allQuestions.text: What is the main finding on this chest radiograph? [img: Radiologycunilateralhilarenlargement.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: The radiograph demonstrates marked enlargement and increased opacity of the left hilum, the normal pulmonary vessels are difficult to delineate. Sarcoidosis classically gives symmetric bilateral hilar nodes, and ipsilateral hilar lymphadenopathy is typical of childhood primary TB.

allQuestions.text: What is the most likely diagnosis? [img: Radiologycthoracicaorticaneurysm.jpg ]
allQuestions.explanation: Axial chest CECT shows fusiform aneurysm involving the ascending thoracic aorta (white solid arrow). Note diameter of the pulmonary trunk (white curved arrow), which normally is approximately the same size as the ascending aorta.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about air bronchograms is FALSE?
options: They are commonly seen in lung consolidation
They are present in alveolar disease
They are absent in pleural effusion
They are typical in lung collapse
They represent patent airways outlined by air within opacified lung
originalOptions: They are commonly seen in lung consolidation
They are present in alveolar disease
They are absent in pleural effusion
They are typical in lung collapse
They represent patent airways outlined by air within opacified lung
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) They are typical in lung collapse
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: They are typical in lung collapse
allQuestions.explanation: Air bronchograms characterize consolidation and alveolar disease. They are not a typical feature of collapse, which is defined by volume loss with crowded bronchi.

allQuestions.text: Air bronchograms are a characteristic finding in which of the following?
allQuestions.explanation: In consolidation the alveoli are filled while the bronchi remain patent, so air-filled bronchi are outlined within the homogeneous opacity. They are absent in effusion and pneumothorax, and collapse is defined by volume loss rather than air bronchograms.

allQuestions.text: All of the following are true about consolidation EXCEPT:
options: It can be caused by bronchoalveolar carcinoma
Volume loss of the affected lung
It may present as lobar or bronchopneumonia
originalOptions: It can be caused by bronchoalveolar carcinoma
Volume loss of the affected lung
It may present as lobar or bronchopneumonia
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Volume loss of the affected lung
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Volume loss of the affected lung
allQuestions.explanation: In consolidation, air is replaced by fluid, pus or cells, so lung volume is preserved. Volume loss indicates collapse.

allQuestions.text: All of the following can cause lobar collapse EXCEPT:
options: Bullous emphysema of the involved lobe
originalOptions: Bullous emphysema of the involved lobe
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) Bullous emphysema of the involved lobe
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Bullous emphysema of the involved lobe
allQuestions.explanation: Lobar collapse results from luminal obstruction (foreign body, mucus plug), mural lesions (carcinoma) or extrinsic compression. Bullous emphysema does not obstruct the supplying bronchus.

allQuestions.text: An infant is suspected of having left-sided foreign body aspiration. Which of the following chest views is NOT helpful?
allQuestions.explanation: With a check-valve obstruction, the affected lung fails to deflate on expiration or when the affected side is dependent (left lateral decubitus). A right lateral decubitus view gives no additional information for a left-sided foreign body.

allQuestions.text: Regarding the pathology seen on the provided image, which of the following is TRUE? [img: Radiologyclobarconsolidation.png ]
options: Mediastinal shift to the same side aids the diagnosis of consolidation
The presence of air bronchograms aids the diagnosis of collapse
Lobar consolidation is usually bordered by a lung fissure
Clear outline of adjacent structures aids the diagnosis of pleural fluid
Volume loss of the affected lobe is the hallmark of consolidation

Lobar consolidation is usually bordered by a lung fissure

allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Lobar consolidation is usually bordered by a lung fissure
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Lobar consolidation is usually bordered by a lung fissure
allQuestions.explanation: Lobar consolidation is sharply demarcated by the fissure. Shift toward the lesion and volume loss suggest collapse, and effusion obscures adjacent structures.

allQuestions.text: Regarding the provided image, what is the best management for the pathology seen? [img: Radiologycpneumoniamanagement.png ]
allQuestions.explanation: The image shows consolidation from bacterial pneumonia, which is treated with antibiotics. A chest tube is for pneumothorax or empyema, and diuretics are for pulmonary edema in heart failure.

allQuestions.text: Regarding pneumothorax, which of the following is TRUE?
options: Mediastinal shift to the left is usually associated with left tension pneumothorax
Cavitary neoplasms are the usual cause of primary pneumothorax
The chest tube should be inserted anterosuperiorly at the affected side
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs in short elderly women

Cavitary neoplasms are the usual cause of primary pneumothorax
The chest tube should be inserted anterosuperiorly at the affected side
Primary spontaneous pneumothorax typically occurs in short elderly women
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The chest tube should be inserted anterosuperiorly at the affected side
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The chest tube should be inserted anterosuperiorly at the affected side
allQuestions.explanation: Air collects anteriorly and superiorly, so the tube is placed there. Laceration causes an ipsilateral pneumothorax, tension pushes the mediastinum away, and primary spontaneous pneumothorax affects tall young patients.

allQuestions.text: Regarding pneumothorax, which of the following is TRUE?
options: The chest tube should be inserted posterosuperiorly at the affected side
The affected lung shows increased lucency in tension pneumothorax
The chest tube should be inserted posteroinferiorly at the affected side
The chest tube should be placed anteroinferiorly at the affected side
The mediastinum shifts toward the side of the tension pneumothorax
originalOptions: The chest tube should be inserted posterosuperiorly at the affected side
The affected lung shows increased lucency in tension pneumothorax
The chest tube should be inserted posteroinferiorly at the affected side
The chest tube should be placed anteroinferiorly at the affected side
The mediastinum shifts toward the side of the tension pneumothorax
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The affected lung shows increased lucency in tension pneumothorax
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The affected lung shows increased lucency in tension pneumothorax
allQuestions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax gives a hyperlucent hemithorax with a collapsed lung. The mediastinum shifts away from it, and the tube is placed anterosuperiorly, not posteriorly or inferiorly.

allQuestions.text: Regarding normal appearances on chest imaging, which of the following is TRUE?
options: The left main bronchus is shorter and steeper than the right main bronchus
The heart base consists of the right atrium shadow
The right vascular bulge at the third intercostal space represents the aortic knob
The right pulmonary artery arches over the right main bronchus
The right hemidiaphragm is normally higher than the left (up to about 2 cm)

The heart base consists of the right atrium shadow

The right pulmonary artery arches over the right main bronchus
The right hemidiaphragm is normally higher than the left (up to about 2 cm)
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) The right hemidiaphragm is normally higher than the left (up to about 2 cm)
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The right hemidiaphragm is normally higher than the left (up to about 2 cm)
allQuestions.explanation: The liver normally elevates the right hemidiaphragm. The left main bronchus is longer and more horizontal, and the aortic knob lies on the left.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about stage II sarcoidosis is WRONG?
options: Hilar lymph node enlargement is present
Nodal enlargement with pleural effusion is the defining feature
Reticulonodular opacities may involve the upper zones

Nodal enlargement with pleural effusion is the defining feature
Reticulonodular opacities may involve the upper zones
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) Nodal enlargement with pleural effusion is the defining feature
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Nodal enlargement with pleural effusion is the defining feature
allQuestions.explanation: Stage II is defined by nodal enlargement plus parenchymal disease. Pleural effusion is not a staging criterion.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is WRONG regarding cavitation in post-primary tuberculosis?
options: It is more likely to occur than in primary TB
It develops mainly in the posterior segments of the upper lobes
The superior segment of the lower lobe can also be involved
It develops years after the primary infection, often with decreased immunity
It typically occurs in the posterior basal segments of the lower lobes

It develops mainly in the posterior segments of the upper lobes
The superior segment of the lower lobe can also be involved
It develops years after the primary infection, often with decreased immunity
It typically occurs in the posterior basal segments of the lower lobes
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) It typically occurs in the posterior basal segments of the lower lobes
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It typically occurs in the posterior basal segments of the lower lobes
allQuestions.explanation: Post-primary cavities occur in the posterior segments of the upper lobes (~85%) and the superior segment of the lower lobe. The posterior basal segments are not typical.

allQuestions.text: Why does the heart appear magnified on an AP chest radiograph?
options: The scapulae overlie the cardiac shadow
The patient is usually rotated during the examination
The heart is farther from the detector
The beam traverses the patient from posterior to anterior
The lungs are hyperinflated on AP films
originalOptions: The scapulae overlie the cardiac shadow
The patient is usually rotated during the examination
The heart is farther from the detector
The beam traverses the patient from posterior to anterior
The lungs are hyperinflated on AP films
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The heart is farther from the detector
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The heart is farther from the detector
allQuestions.explanation: Magnification is geometric, because in the AP view the heart lies farther from the detector than in the PA view. Rotation and overlying scapulae are drawbacks of AP films but are not the cause of magnification, and a posterior-to-anterior beam describes the PA view.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following typically causes mediastinal shift AWAY from the affected side?
options: Complete obstruction of the main bronchus
originalOptions: Complete obstruction of the main bronchus
allQuestions.explanation: A large effusion exerts mass effect and pushes the mediastinum away from the affected side. Collapse (including complete main bronchus obstruction) pulls the mediastinum toward the affected side, consolidation preserves volume without shift, and a simple pneumothorax causes no shift unless it becomes tension.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a characteristic sign of pleural effusion on an erect frontal chest radiograph?
allQuestions.explanation: Fluid climbs the lateral chest wall, forming a concave-upward meniscus that slopes gently medially, together with blunting of the costophrenic angle. Air bronchogram indicates consolidation, signet ring indicates bronchiectasis, and cephalization and Kerley B lines are features of heart failure.

allQuestions.text: Regarding the thin white line seen on an erect chest radiograph in pneumothorax, which of the following is TRUE?
options: Lung markings extend peripheral to the line
The peripheral space is radiolucent compared with the adjacent lung
The line represents the parietal pleura
The mediastinum always shifts away from the affected side
The peripheral space appears denser than the adjacent lung
originalOptions: Lung markings extend peripheral to the line
The peripheral space is radiolucent compared with the adjacent lung
The line represents the parietal pleura
The mediastinum always shifts away from the affected side
The peripheral space appears denser than the adjacent lung
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The peripheral space is radiolucent compared with the adjacent lung
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The peripheral space is radiolucent compared with the adjacent lung
allQuestions.explanation: The line is the visceral pleural edge, and the air-filled pleural space beyond it is lucent and avascular. Shift away from the pneumothorax occurs only in tension pneumothorax.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is TRUE regarding heart failure on chest radiography?
options: Pleural effusions are not a feature
Cephalization of the pulmonary vessels is seen
Kerley B lines are long lines at the lung apices
The cardiothoracic ratio is typically below 50%
originalOptions: Pleural effusions are not a feature
Cephalization of the pulmonary vessels is seen
Kerley B lines are long lines at the lung apices
The cardiothoracic ratio is typically below 50%
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) Cephalization of the pulmonary vessels is seen
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: Cephalization of the pulmonary vessels is seen
allQuestions.explanation: Pulmonary venous congestion dilates the upper lobe veins (cephalization). Heart failure causes cardiomegaly (cardiothoracic ratio >50%) and effusions, and Kerley B lines are 1–2 cm peripheral lines at the lung bases, not the apices.

allQuestions.text: A chest radiograph shows a thin visceral pleural line with absent lung markings peripheral to it and no mediastinal shift. What is the most likely diagnosis?
allQuestions.explanation: A visible visceral pleural edge with an avascular lucent space beyond it is diagnostic of pneumothorax, and the absence of mediastinal shift makes it non-tension. Tension pneumothorax shifts the mediastinum away, and effusion, collapse and consolidation all produce opacity.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is WRONG regarding pleural effusion?
options: Blunting of the costophrenic angle is seen
A meniscus is seen on erect frontal films
A lateral decubitus view with the affected side down is the most sensitive projection

allQuestions.explanation: Fluid is soft-tissue density, so an effusion appears as an opacity (white). Pneumothorax is the pleural pathology that appears lucent.

allQuestions.text: Which is NOT a feature of a simple bone cyst?

allQuestions.explanation: A colloid cyst at the foramen of Monro physically obstructs CSF flow (non-communicating hydrocephalus); SAH, meningitis, and meningeal carcinomatosis impair CSF absorption (communicating), and choroid plexus papilloma causes communicating hydrocephalus via CSF overproduction.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following does NOT show restricted diffusion on MRI (DWI)?

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause of restriction on diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI)?
allQuestions.explanation: Arachnoid cysts contain simple CSF-like fluid and do not restrict diffusion, unlike abscesses, acute ischemia, high-grade tumors, and post-ictal states.

allQuestions.text: A brain MRI lesion is isointense on T1 and hyperintense on T2. What stage of hemorrhage is most likely?
allQuestions.explanation: Intracellular oxyhemoglobin in the hyperacute stage is T1 isointense and T2 hyperintense; acute (deoxyhemoglobin) blood is instead T2 hypointense.

allQuestions.text: A patient presents with seizures. Which of the following brain tumors is most commonly associated with seizures?
allQuestions.explanation: Oligodendrogliomas characteristically involve the cortex/subcortical white matter, making seizures a very common presenting symptom compared with the other listed tumors.

allQuestions.text: Which brain tumor is characteristically associated with a "butterfly" pattern on imaging?
allQuestions.explanation: GBM classically spreads across the corpus callosum, producing a bilateral, symmetric "butterfly glioma" appearance not typical of the other tumors.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a recognized cause of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)?
allQuestions.explanation: Meningioma is not a recognized cause of SAH; trauma, ruptured aneurysm, and vasculitis are the classic causes.

allQuestions.text: Which of the statements about intracranial dural venous sinuses is FALSE?

allQuestions.text: What is the most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?

allQuestions.text: All of the following can present in neurofibromatosis type 2, EXCEPT:

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is a white matter structure?

allQuestions.text: All of the following appear hyperintense on T2 MRI, EXCEPT:
allQuestions.explanation: Air produces a signal void and appears hypointense on all MRI sequences, unlike fatty marrow, late subacute hematoma, choroid plexus papilloma, and GBM, which are typically T2 hyperintense.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT found in hyperacute brain ischemia?
options: Loss of the insular ribbon sign

allQuestions.text: Which of the following sutures joins the parietal bones with the occipital bone?
allQuestions.explanation: The lambdoid suture joins both parietal bones with the occipital bone posteriorly; coronal joins frontal to parietal, sagittal joins the two parietals, and metopic joins the two frontal bones.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following sutures joins the frontal and parietal bones?
allQuestions.explanation: The coronal suture joins the frontal and parietal bones, distinct from the squamosal suture which joins the temporal and parietal bones, the metopic suture which joins the two frontal bones, the sagittal suture which joins the two parietal bones, and the lambdoid suture which joins the occipital and parietal bones.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following sutures joins the two parietal bones?
allQuestions.explanation: The sagittal suture runs in the midline joining the two parietal bones to each other.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following sutures joins the two frontal bones?
allQuestions.explanation: The metopic suture is the embryological midline suture between the two frontal bones, which normally fuses in early childhood.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following radiologic features, if present, is supportive of the diagnosis of Sturge-Weber syndrome?

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about the Circle of Willis is FALSE?

allQuestions.explanation: AICA is a branch of the proximal basilar artery; the distal vertebral artery instead gives rise to PICA. SCA does arise from the distal basilar artery, and the Circle of Willis does provide interhemispheric collateral flow.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is WRONG regarding cranial nerve involvement in multiple sclerosis?

The abducens nerve (CN6) can be affected
Optic nerve involvement (optic neuritis) is common
originalOptions: The trigeminal nerve (CN5) can be affected
The oculomotor nerve is the most commonly affected cranial nerve
The abducens nerve (CN6) can be affected
Optic nerve involvement (optic neuritis) is common
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) The oculomotor nerve is the most commonly affected cranial nerve
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The oculomotor nerve is the most commonly affected cranial nerve
allQuestions.explanation: Optic neuritis (CN2) is the most common cranial nerve manifestation of MS, followed by CN5/6; oculomotor involvement is not the classic pattern.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about MS lesion characteristics is TRUE?
options: Active plaques characteristically do not enhance with contrast
Diffuse cerebral atrophy is an early MS finding
T1-hypointense "black hole" lesions indicate a better prognosis
Enhancement never occurs in MS lesions
T1-hypointense lesions ("black holes") correlate with axonal destruction and a worse prognosis
originalOptions: Active plaques characteristically do not enhance with contrast
Diffuse cerebral atrophy is an early MS finding
T1-hypointense "black hole" lesions indicate a better prognosis
Enhancement never occurs in MS lesions
T1-hypointense lesions ("black holes") correlate with axonal destruction and a worse prognosis
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) T1-hypointense lesions ("black holes") correlate with axonal destruction and a worse prognosis
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: T1-hypointense lesions ("black holes") correlate with axonal destruction and a worse prognosis
allQuestions.explanation: T1 hypointensity reflects irreversible axonal loss; active plaques classically DO enhance (reflecting blood-brain barrier breakdown), and diffuse atrophy is typically a late finding.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following statements about primary CNS lymphoma is FALSE?
options: It is typically hyperdense on non-contrast CT
It shows restricted diffusion on DWI
The ADC value is higher than normal brain parenchyma
It shows homogeneous enhancement in immunocompetent patients
originalOptions: It is typically hyperdense on non-contrast CT
It shows restricted diffusion on DWI
The ADC value is higher than normal brain parenchyma
It shows homogeneous enhancement in immunocompetent patients
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The ADC value is higher than normal brain parenchyma
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The ADC value is higher than normal brain parenchyma
allQuestions.explanation: Primary CNS lymphoma is highly cellular and restricts diffusion, so its ADC value is typically LOWER, not higher, than normal brain.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following anatomical relationships is CORRECT?
options: The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
The hippocampus lies anterosuperior to the amygdala
The uncus forms the lateral border of the temporal lobe
The claustrum lies medial to the putamen, separated by the internal capsule
originalOptions: The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
The hippocampus lies anterosuperior to the amygdala
The uncus forms the lateral border of the temporal lobe
The claustrum lies medial to the putamen, separated by the internal capsule
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The claustrum lies lateral to the insula
allQuestions.explanation: The claustrum is a thin sheet of grey matter lateral to the insula (separated by the extreme capsule); the hippocampus lies posteroinferior (not anterosuperior) to the amygdala, and the uncus is the medial (not lateral) temporal border.

allQuestions.text: On T1-weighted MRI, which of the following statements about basal ganglia signal is TRUE?
options: The putamen is hyperintense relative to the globus pallidus
The caudate is hyperintense relative to the thalamus
The globus pallidus is isointense to the putamen
The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
originalOptions: The putamen is hyperintense relative to the globus pallidus
The caudate is hyperintense relative to the thalamus
The globus pallidus is isointense to the putamen
The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
allQuestions.correctAnswer: D) The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The globus pallidus is hyperintense relative to the putamen
allQuestions.explanation: On T1-weighted MRI, the globus pallidus normally appears relatively hyperintense compared with the putamen — a useful anatomical landmark.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following locations is NOT typical for hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?
allQuestions.explanation: Hypertensive ICH classically occurs in deep structures (basal ganglia, thalamus, pons, cerebellum) supplied by small penetrating vessels; a lobar location like the frontal lobe instead suggests another etiology (e.g., amyloid angiopathy, AVM, tumor).

allQuestions.text: Which stage of hemorrhage is classically hyperintense on both T1 and T2-weighted MRI due to extracellular methemoglobin?
allQuestions.explanation: Late subacute hemorrhage (extracellular methemoglobin) is T1 and T2 hyperintense; early subacute (intracellular methemoglobin) is T1 hyperintense but T2 hypointense, and acute/chronic stages are T2 hypointense.

allQuestions.text: Regarding cerebral sinus thrombosis, which of the following is TRUE?
options: Sinus thrombosis is an occlusion of arterial channels in the cranial cavity
The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
The dura typically does not enhance
A hypodense sinus is seen on non-contrast CT
originalOptions: Sinus thrombosis is an occlusion of arterial channels in the cranial cavity
The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
The dura typically does not enhance
A hypodense sinus is seen on non-contrast CT
allQuestions.correctAnswer: C) The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: The empty delta sign is a common radiological finding on T1 MRI with contrast
allQuestions.explanation: The empty delta sign — a triangular filling defect surrounded by enhancing dura — is classically seen on contrast-enhanced imaging; sinus thrombosis is a venous (not arterial) occlusion, acute thrombus typically does NOT enhance, the dura DOES enhance, and non-contrast CT shows a hyperdense (not hypodense) sinus.

allQuestions.text: Regarding subdural hematoma, which of the following is TRUE?
options: It does not cross the falx cerebri
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
originalOptions: It does not cross the falx cerebri
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.explanation: Subdural hematoma is confined by the falx cerebri and tentorium but CAN cross suture lines (opposite epidural hematoma); it is typically caused by bridging vein tears (not the middle meningeal artery) and has a crescentic (not lenticular) shape.

allQuestions.text: Regarding extradural (epidural) hematoma, which of the following is FALSE?
options: It does not cross the falx cerebri
There is a history of trauma
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
originalOptions: It does not cross the falx cerebri
There is a history of trauma
It forms between the inner skull table and the outer dural layer
It is usually caused by a tear in the middle meningeal artery
allQuestions.correctAnswer: A) It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: It does not cross the falx cerebri
allQuestions.explanation: Epidural hematoma CAN cross the falx cerebri but does NOT cross cranial sutures (opposite the pattern of subdural hematoma); the other listed features are true.

allQuestions.text: Which one of the following is a common radiologic feature of diffuse brain edema?
allQuestions.explanation: Diffuse cerebral edema effaces the sulci and narrows the ventricles/basal cisterns; the brain typically appears diffusely hypodense (not hyperdense) except for the relatively dense-appearing cerebellum.

questions.text: Under Jordanian law, abortion is permitted under which of the following circumstances?
options: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
originalOptions: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
questions.correctAnswer: B) When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
questions.correctAnswerText: When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
questions.explanation: Jordanian law criminalizes abortion except when continuing the pregnancy would seriously endanger the mother's life or health; it is not permitted on demand, for socioeconomic reasons, or for fetal anomaly alone.

questions.text: Abortion in Jordanian law is allowed:
options: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
originalOptions: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
questions.correctAnswer: E) To save the mother's life
questions.explanation: Under the Jordan Penal Code, abortion is a criminal offense except when continuation of pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause or indicator of child abuse?
questions.explanation: MS is a neurological autoimmune disease unrelated to abuse; multiple bruises, shaken baby syndrome, and Munchausen by proxy are classic abuse indicators.

questions.text: Bruising in which of the following areas is NOT considered a suspicious sign of child abuse?
questions.explanation: Knee bruising is a common, normal childhood injury from falls and play; abuse-related bruising is characteristically found on protected areas such as the torso, back, abdomen, and chest.

questions.text: Regarding Munchausen syndrome by proxy, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Illness does not suggest a particular disease
The child becomes ill in the presence of the caregiver
Laboratory and radiographic findings are negative
Parents readily admit to causing the illness
originalOptions: Illness does not suggest a particular disease
The child becomes ill in the presence of the caregiver
Laboratory and radiographic findings are negative
Parents readily admit to causing the illness
questions.correctAnswer: D) Parents readily admit to causing the illness
questions.correctAnswerText: Parents readily admit to causing the illness
questions.explanation: Munchausen by proxy is characterized by unexplained illness that improves when the child is separated from the caregiver, a lack of clear diagnosis, and negative workup; perpetrators rarely confess to causing the illness.

questions.text: A 31-year-old woman claims sexual assault 4 days ago. Examination shows a recent hymenal tear at the 5 o'clock position. Which statement is TRUE?
options: No informed consent is required before examination
Delay in reporting confirms a fabricated story
Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
Rupture of the hymen is an absolute sign confirming rape
The findings determine the exact time of the assault
originalOptions: No informed consent is required before examination
Delay in reporting confirms a fabricated story
Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
Rupture of the hymen is an absolute sign confirming rape
The findings determine the exact time of the assault
questions.correctAnswer: C) Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
questions.correctAnswerText: Signs of injury corroborate and support the claim, though not confirmatory alone
questions.explanation: A recent hymenal tear is corroborative evidence supporting the allegation, but it alone cannot confirm rape; consent is required before examination, and delayed reporting is common even in genuine cases.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT true concerning sexual assault victims?
options: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
Post-assault forensic sampling is vital for evaluation
Victims should be assessed for genitourinary health, contraception needs, and counseling
Emergency contraception may include oral contraceptives
originalOptions: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
Post-assault forensic sampling is vital for evaluation
Victims should be assessed for genitourinary health, contraception needs, and counseling
Emergency contraception may include oral contraceptives
questions.correctAnswer: A) Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
questions.correctAnswerText: Bestiality/paedophilia is a common practice among 30% of young adults
questions.explanation: This statistic is false — paedophilia and bestiality are not common practices in any population; the other statements reflect appropriate sexual assault management.

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized type of hymen?
questions.explanation: Cribriform hymen (with multiple small openings) is a recognized anatomical variant; notches at 3 or 9 o'clock are considered normal artefacts rather than named types, and "elastic" is not a recognized hymen type.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of erectile dysfunction (impotence) in young men?
questions.explanation: In young men, erectile dysfunction is most commonly psychogenic in origin, whereas vascular causes become more predominant with advancing age.

questions.text: Which of the following deaths is classified as a medico-legal case requiring investigation?
options: Death occurring while in prison/state custody
Death from a known natural disease at home
Hospital death from a previously diagnosed disease
Death from chronic illness under stable medical care
originalOptions: Death occurring while in prison/state custody
Death from a known natural disease at home
Hospital death from a previously diagnosed disease
Death from chronic illness under stable medical care
questions.correctAnswer: A) Death occurring while in prison/state custody
questions.correctAnswerText: Death occurring while in prison/state custody
questions.explanation: All deaths occurring in state custody must be investigated as medico-legal cases to rule out foul play and ensure accountability, unlike expected natural deaths under known medical care.

questions.text: Which of the following can cause myocardial infarction WITHOUT underlying atheroma?
options: Intense emotional stress causing coronary vasospasm
originalOptions: Intense emotional stress causing coronary vasospasm
questions.correctAnswer: C) Intense emotional stress causing coronary vasospasm
questions.correctAnswerText: Intense emotional stress causing coronary vasospasm
questions.explanation: Severe emotional stress can trigger Prinzmetal-type coronary vasospasm, producing MI in the absence of atherosclerotic plaque — a medico-legally significant distinction from atheroma-driven causes like hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes.

questions.text: A person dies in prison from bronchospasm. What is the correct course of action?
options: The physician must legally report the death to the public prosecutor
A standard death certificate is sufficient
Family consent is needed before autopsy
originalOptions: The physician must legally report the death to the public prosecutor
A standard death certificate is sufficient
Family consent is needed before autopsy
questions.correctAnswer: A) The physician must legally report the death to the public prosecutor
questions.correctAnswerText: The physician must legally report the death to the public prosecutor
questions.explanation: Deaths in state custody are mandatory medico-legal cases; the physician is legally obligated to notify the public prosecutor regardless of the apparent cause of death.

questions.text: Which of the following causes of death is NOT considered medico-legal?
options: Pulmonary embolism following hip fracture in hospital
Pneumonia in a 16-year-old in a juvenile detention facility
Tuberculosis death in a 30-year-old refugee under active medical care
Sudden death of a 60-year-old while awaiting an X-ray
originalOptions: Pulmonary embolism following hip fracture in hospital
Pneumonia in a 16-year-old in a juvenile detention facility
Tuberculosis death in a 30-year-old refugee under active medical care
Sudden death of a 60-year-old while awaiting an X-ray
questions.correctAnswer: D) Tuberculosis death in a 30-year-old refugee under active medical care
questions.correctAnswerText: Tuberculosis death in a 30-year-old refugee under active medical care
questions.explanation: Death from tuberculosis under active, established medical care represents an expected natural death; the other scenarios involve trauma, custodial settings, or unexplained sudden death, all of which qualify as medico-legal.

questions.text: When a forensic physician is called to a scene by the public prosecutor, what are the PRIMARY purposes?
options: Identification of the deceased and investigation of the circumstances of death
To clean and document the scene
originalOptions: Identification of the deceased and investigation of the circumstances of death
To clean and document the scene
questions.correctAnswer: B) Identification of the deceased and investigation of the circumstances of death
questions.correctAnswerText: Identification of the deceased and investigation of the circumstances of death
questions.explanation: The forensic physician's scene role centers on identifying the body and estimating the time, cause, and manner of death to help reconstruct events for the prosecutor, rather than the narrower or unrelated tasks listed.

questions.text: Which stage of lobar pneumonia is most likely to cause death in children?
questions.explanation: The congestion stage causes the most severe toxemia and is the most dangerous phase of lobar pneumonia, particularly in children, compared to the later hepatization and resolution stages.

questions.text: What is the most common cause of sudden unexpected death?
questions.explanation: Coronary artery disease, acute myocardial infarction, and hypertensive heart disease together account for the majority of sudden unexpected deaths in adults, outweighing respiratory, CNS, or metabolic causes.

questions.text: When dealing with vulnerable children (victims of violence), what is the MAIN priority of the physician from an ethical point of view?
questions.explanation: The physician's primary ethical duty with child abuse victims is early identification and protection, which takes priority over confidentiality or parental autonomy.

questions.text: Breach of confidentiality is permissible in which case?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Upon request of the patient
questions.explanation: Confidentiality may be breached with the patient's own consent, for notifiable diseases, court order, or public safety — spousal, insurer, or employer requests without patient consent do not justify it.

questions.text: Breaching confidentiality is permissible in:
questions.explanation: Notifiable/communicable diseases like cholera must be reported to public health authorities by law regardless of patient consent, due to public health risk.

questions.text: All but one of the following is related to the bioethics principles (code of ethics):
questions.explanation: The four bioethics pillars are autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence, and justice; "reluctant" is not a recognized bioethical principle.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT correct concerning valid consent prior to medical treatment:
options: Consent of partner (Husband/Wife) is always mandatory
Informed of what the treatment involves
originalOptions: Consent of partner (Husband/Wife) is always mandatory
Informed of what the treatment involves
questions.correctAnswer: B) Consent of partner (Husband/Wife) is always mandatory
questions.correctAnswerText: Consent of partner (Husband/Wife) is always mandatory
questions.explanation: A competent adult patient can independently give valid consent; requiring spousal consent would violate patient autonomy.

questions.text: Regarding consent — a 23-year-old single adult female with vaginal bleeding. Which statement is correct?
options: Medical consent must be obtained from her father or husband
Consent of partner is always mandatory
An adult patient can give her own medical consent independently
originalOptions: Medical consent must be obtained from her father or husband
Consent of partner is always mandatory
An adult patient can give her own medical consent independently
questions.correctAnswer: D) An adult patient can give her own medical consent independently
questions.correctAnswerText: An adult patient can give her own medical consent independently
questions.explanation: Any competent adult has full legal capacity to consent to medical treatment without parental or spousal authorization.

questions.text: The utmost important rule when doing a physical examination of intimate parts of the body is:
options: Only a same-sex physician may examine
A family member must be present
originalOptions: Only a same-sex physician may examine
A family member must be present
questions.correctAnswer: A) A chaperon must be present
questions.explanation: A chaperon safeguards both the patient's dignity and the physician's professional integrity during intimate examinations.

questions.text: "Respect for Persons" in the ethical approach might mean any of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Respect for persons centers on autonomy, integrity, equity, and equality, which empower the patient — blind obedience to the doctor is the opposite of patient-centred ethics.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT TRUE concerning duties of doctors to patients:
options: Respect a patient's right to confidentiality
Always bear in mind the obligation to respect human life
Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
Whenever examination is beyond the physician's capacity, refer to another physician
Act in the patient's best interest when providing medical care
originalOptions: Respect a patient's right to confidentiality
Always bear in mind the obligation to respect human life
Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
Whenever examination is beyond the physician's capacity, refer to another physician
Act in the patient's best interest when providing medical care
questions.correctAnswer: C) Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
questions.correctAnswerText: Informed consent is not necessary when dealing with victims of violence
questions.explanation: Informed consent is always required except in true emergencies where delay would cause harm; being a violence victim does not remove this requirement.

questions.text: One of the following characters is NOT appropriate considering ethical standards:
questions.correctAnswer: B) Enhance intimate relationships with patients
questions.explanation: Romantic or intimate relationships between physicians and patients violate professional boundaries and are strictly unethical.

questions.text: One of the following is odd and not known to be relevant to world medical declarations related to humanization of health service:
options: United Nations development fund for women
originalOptions: United Nations development fund for women
questions.correctAnswer: B) United Nations development fund for women
questions.correctAnswerText: United Nations development fund for women
questions.explanation: Recognized WHO/WMA medical declarations include Helsinki and Geneva; the UN development fund for women is not a medical declaration.

questions.text: One of the following is odd and not well known to be relevant to world medical declarations related to humanization of health service:
questions.explanation: WMA declarations include Geneva, Helsinki, Oslo, and Tokyo; there is no formally recognized "Declaration of London" in medical ethics.

questions.text: Humanization of medical practice was the main theme in:
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Geneva (1948) was the WMA's post-WWII commitment to humanize medical practice, forming the modern physician's oath.

questions.text: Declaration of Helsinki is related to:
questions.explanation: The Declaration of Helsinki (1964) establishes ethical standards specifically for medical research involving human subjects.

questions.text: Types of consent — all EXCEPT one:
options: Involvement in a research trial authorized by IRB
originalOptions: Involvement in a research trial authorized by IRB
questions.explanation: Euthanasia is not a valid consent scenario for treatment — it is illegal in most jurisdictions, unlike the other listed valid consent types.

questions.text: What type of toxicology concerns itself with medical and legal aspects, focused on detecting poisons in medicolegal investigations?
questions.explanation: Forensic toxicology represents the intersection of toxicology with the law, applying poison detection specifically to medicolegal investigations, distinguishing it from clinical (patient management), environmental, and purely analytical toxicology.

questions.text: What color is associated with methemoglobin?
questions.explanation: Methemoglobin (Fe³⁺ state) produces a characteristic chocolate-brown discoloration of blood and livor, and causes cyanosis that fails to improve with supplemental oxygen — distinguishing it from cherry-red (carbon monoxide) or cyanotic bluish-purple (hypoxia) presentations.

questions.text: Activated charcoal is useless in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal effectively adsorbs salicylates (along with paracetamol and tricyclics), but it is ineffective for iron, lithium, cyanide, corrosives, alcohols, and heavy metals.

questions.text: Which of the following substances is best absorbed (adsorbed) by activated charcoal?
questions.explanation: Salicylate is well adsorbed by activated charcoal, whereas iron, lithium, and cyanide are not effectively bound by it.

questions.text: Which statement about activated charcoal is TRUE?
options: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
It works by absorption into the toxin
It is contraindicated in all cases of poisoning
originalOptions: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
It works by absorption into the toxin
It is contraindicated in all cases of poisoning
questions.correctAnswer: A) It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
questions.correctAnswerText: It reduces poison absorption by adsorbing it in the GI lumen
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal works via adsorption — binding the toxin to its surface in the gut — thereby preventing systemic absorption, rather than being absorbed itself or inducing emesis.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about activated charcoal is FALSE?
options: It should be given as soon as possible after ingestion
It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
It works by adsorbing toxins in the gut
It is ineffective for metals and alcohols
originalOptions: It should be given as soon as possible after ingestion
It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
It works by adsorbing toxins in the gut
It is ineffective for metals and alcohols
questions.correctAnswer: B) It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
questions.correctAnswerText: It can be combined with syrup of ipecac to induce vomiting
questions.explanation: Activated charcoal and syrup of ipecac should never be combined, since ipecac-induced vomiting would expel the charcoal from the stomach before it can adsorb the toxin.

questions.text: All of the following are true about activated charcoal EXCEPT:
options: Give with a sufficient amount of water
It is a finely arranged black powder
Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
originalOptions: Give with a sufficient amount of water
It is a finely arranged black powder
Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
questions.correctAnswer: C) Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
questions.correctAnswerText: Given with syrup of ipecac to increase effectiveness
questions.explanation: Ipecac is not routinely recommended and should never be combined with activated charcoal, as it would counteract the charcoal's effect by inducing vomiting rather than improving efficacy.

questions.text: A patient arrives at the ER 2 hours after an overdose. What is the correct management?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Activated charcoal if no contraindications
questions.explanation: Within 2 hours of ingestion, activated charcoal is first-line if the airway is intact and there are no contraindications; syrup of ipecac is no longer recommended, and gastric lavage is rarely used (limited to within about 1 hour with a protected airway).

questions.text: Why are alkaline (base) burns generally MORE dangerous than acidic burns?
options: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
They cause coagulative necrosis, which limits penetration
Acids are neutralized immediately upon contact
Bases do not penetrate mucous membranes
originalOptions: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
They cause coagulative necrosis, which limits penetration
Acids are neutralized immediately upon contact
Bases do not penetrate mucous membranes
questions.correctAnswer: A) They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
questions.correctAnswerText: They cause liquefactive necrosis, allowing deeper tissue penetration
questions.explanation: Alkalis dissolve proteins and saponify fat, producing liquefactive necrosis without a limiting eschar, allowing progressively deeper tissue injury; acids instead cause coagulative necrosis, which forms a protective eschar that limits further penetration.

questions.text: Which specific enzyme is reactivated after organophosphate poisoning (before aging)?
questions.explanation: OP poisons phosphorylate AChE; before "aging" occurs (~48h), pralidoxime can remove the phosphoryl group and restore enzyme activity.

questions.text: The drug that reactivates phosphorylated AChE in organophosphate poisoning (before aging):
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime is an oxime AChE reactivator effective only before aging; atropine blocks muscarinic effects but does not reactivate the enzyme.

questions.text: Enzyme reactivated by pralidoxime in organophosphate poisoning:
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime specifically reactivates AChE (not pseudocholinesterase/BuChE), and only before the phosphorylated enzyme ages.

questions.text: Which of the following statements about carbamate and organophosphate poisoning is FALSE?
options: Both cause muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms
Atropine is used for symptomatic treatment
Both can lead to respiratory failure
originalOptions: Both cause muscarinic and nicotinic symptoms
Atropine is used for symptomatic treatment
Both can lead to respiratory failure
questions.correctAnswer: D) Both are treated with pralidoxime
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime is not indicated for carbamate poisoning because carbamate-enzyme inhibition does not undergo aging (it's spontaneously reversible), unlike OP poisoning.

questions.text: Management of carbamate toxicity – all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
originalOptions: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
questions.correctAnswer: B) Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
questions.correctAnswerText: Starting treatment should be delayed until level of anti-cholinesterase is known
questions.explanation: Treatment (ABC + atropine) must never be delayed for lab confirmation in cholinesterase-inhibitor poisoning, as this is a time-critical emergency.

questions.text: Not a muscarinic sign of organophosphate poisoning:
questions.explanation: Muscarinic (SLUDGE) effects cause urinary incontinence/frequency; urinary retention instead reflects a nicotinic/sympathetic effect.

questions.text: What is the role of atropine in the treatment of organophosphate poisoning?
questions.explanation: Atropine is a competitive muscarinic antagonist that dries secretions and reverses muscarinic toxicity; it has no effect on nicotinic weakness, which requires pralidoxime.

questions.text: Management and treatment of organophosphate poisoning – which is TRUE:
options: Atropine is antidote for nicotinic receptor
originalOptions: Atropine is antidote for nicotinic receptor
questions.explanation: Initial priority is airway management including suctioning of bronchial secretions, followed by atropine for muscarinic symptoms and then pralidoxime.

questions.text: Low dose of organophosphates is NOT associated with:
questions.explanation: Low-dose OP exposure produces muscarinic effects (bronchorrhea, miosis, salivation); paralysis is a nicotinic effect seen at high dose.

questions.text: Organophosphate-induced neuropsychiatric disorder (OPIDP) happens:
questions.correctAnswer: B) After 1-5 weeks of OP poisoning
questions.explanation: OPIDP is a delayed peripheral polyneuropathy appearing 1–5 weeks post-exposure, distinct from the immediate cholinergic crisis and the 24–96h intermediate syndrome.

questions.text: Antidote of organophosphate poisoning:
questions.explanation: Dual therapy is required — atropine blocks muscarinic toxicity while pralidoxime reactivates AChE, addressing nicotinic and central effects.

questions.text: What is the best blood sample site for forensic toxicology analysis?
questions.explanation: Femoral vein blood is preferred postmortem because it is peripheral and less affected by postmortem redistribution (PMR), unlike central sites (subclavian, jugular) that are subject to drug diffusion from nearby organs.

questions.text: Which sample site is best for QUANTITATIVE toxicology analysis?
questions.explanation: Femoral blood undergoes minimal postmortem redistribution, making it the preferred site for accurate quantitative drug measurement, whereas central blood (heart, subclavian) is prone to redistribution artifact.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT a characteristic of vitreous humor as a toxicology sample?
questions.correctAnswer: B) More susceptible to postmortem change
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is actually resistant to postmortem change because it is isolated behind the blood-ocular barrier, protecting it from putrefaction and postmortem redistribution — making the "more susceptible" statement false.

questions.text: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding vitreous humor in forensic toxicology?
questions.correctAnswer: A) Done as a routine procedure
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is collected only in specific circumstances (decomposed bodies, suspected drug/alcohol use, or when other samples are unavailable), not as a routine procedure.

questions.text: Which of the following CANNOT be determined by analyzing vitreous fluid?
questions.explanation: Vitreous fluid can detect alcohol, glucose, electrolytes, potassium (useful for postmortem interval), and urea/creatinine (renal function), but heavy metals preferentially accumulate in hair, nails, and bone rather than vitreous humor.

questions.text: Which sample is most resistant to postmortem putrefaction, making it valuable in decomposed bodies?
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor's anatomical isolation behind the blood-ocular barrier makes it the most resistant forensic sample to putrefactive change among the options listed.

questions.text: Which statement about vitreous fluid is WRONG?
questions.explanation: Vitreous humor is resistant to (not affected by) putrefaction due to its isolated anatomical location, making this statement false while the others are accurate.

questions.text: Which of the following is INCORRECT regarding liver samples in forensic toxicology?
questions.explanation: The liver actually putrefies relatively quickly and is not protected from decomposition, though it remains valuable for assessing lipophilic drug concentrations and tissue distribution.

questions.text: For qualitative assessment (screening) of forensic samples, which is the preferred sample?
questions.explanation: Urine is preferred for qualitative drug screening via immunoassay, while femoral blood is used for quantitation, vitreous humor for decomposed cases, and hair for chronic exposure history.

questions.text: Which statement about urine samples in forensic toxicology is NOT correct?
options: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
Urine can detect drugs and metabolites
Urine is used for qualitative drug screening
Urine is useful for detecting drug exposure
originalOptions: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
Urine can detect drugs and metabolites
Urine is used for qualitative drug screening
Urine is useful for detecting drug exposure
questions.correctAnswer: A) Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
questions.correctAnswerText: Urine is used for quantitative analysis of most drugs
questions.explanation: Urine is mainly used for qualitative detection of drug exposure, not quantitative measurement, which requires blood analysis.

questions.text: Which of the following is NOT TRUE concerning sodium fluoride as a preservative in forensic blood samples?
options: Inhibits glycolysis, preventing postmortem glucose changes
Used as a preservative in blood samples for alcohol analysis
Prevents postmortem production of alcohol by microorganisms
originalOptions: Inhibits glycolysis, preventing postmortem glucose changes
Used as a preservative in blood samples for alcohol analysis
Prevents postmortem production of alcohol by microorganisms
questions.explanation: Sodium fluoride inhibits bacterial growth and glycolysis, thereby preventing fermentation (and postmortem alcohol production by microorganisms) rather than enhancing it, which is why it is used to preserve blood samples for alcohol analysis.

questions.text: Issuing the initial medical report in a medico-legal case is the responsibility of:
options: The first physician who manages the patient in the emergency department
originalOptions: The first physician who manages the patient in the emergency department
questions.correctAnswer: C) The first physician who manages the patient in the emergency department
questions.correctAnswerText: The first physician who manages the patient in the emergency department
questions.explanation: The primary medico-legal report is always issued by the first doctor to examine the patient, regardless of specialty, to ensure timely and accurate documentation.

questions.text: Who gives the PRIMARY medical report:
options: The first surgeon who met the patient
The first doctor who met the patient
originalOptions: The first surgeon who met the patient
The first doctor who met the patient
questions.correctAnswer: B) The first doctor who met the patient
questions.correctAnswerText: The first doctor who met the patient
questions.explanation: Legal responsibility for the initial medico-legal report falls on the first physician to assess the patient, irrespective of specialty.

questions.text: Reporting and documentation of injuries will include all of the following EXCEPT one:
options: Injury location (anatomical measure distance from landmark)
Assailant description whether left or right hand user
originalOptions: Injury location (anatomical measure distance from landmark)
Assailant description whether left or right hand user
questions.correctAnswer: D) Assailant description whether left or right hand user
questions.correctAnswerText: Assailant description whether left or right hand user
questions.explanation: Medico-legal documentation records the victim's objective injury findings; assailant handedness is an investigative inference, not a clinical documentation item.

questions.text: According to Jordanian Public Health Law, a physician MUST report which of the following to the Ministry of Health:
questions.explanation: Jordanian public health law mandates reporting notifiable/communicable diseases (e.g., cholera, typhoid) to the Ministry of Health, not all trauma or deaths generally.

questions.text: A 60-year-old man underwent arthroscopy and meniscectomy, and died of pulmonary embolism. Which post-op care was NEGLIGENT?
options: Not informed how serious it is if he feels headache
Not informed of the kind of painkillers to use
Not told to have residence within 2 miles of hospital
Not informed of how serious it is if he feels short of breath
Not told the duration of disablement from work
originalOptions: Not informed how serious it is if he feels headache
Not informed of the kind of painkillers to use
Not told to have residence within 2 miles of hospital
Not informed of how serious it is if he feels short of breath
Not told the duration of disablement from work
questions.correctAnswer: D) Not informed of how serious it is if he feels short of breath
questions.correctAnswerText: Not informed of how serious it is if he feels short of breath
questions.explanation: Pulmonary embolism is a known post-surgical complication presenting with dyspnoea; failing to warn the patient about this warning sign constitutes negligence.

questions.text: A surgeon under the effect of alcohol performed a laparotomy, resulting in the patient's death. The surgeon is guilty of:
questions.explanation: Operating while impaired by alcohol is a reckless disregard for patient safety with full knowledge of the risk, rising to the level of criminal negligence rather than mere civil liability.

questions.text: Components of a medico-legal report are:
questions.explanation: A complete medico-legal report consists of three parts: the preamble (who/what/when/where), the body of objective findings, and the conclusion containing professional opinion.

questions.text: In Jordan, a physician is legally governed by:
options: Medical Association Law + Public Health Law + Jordanian Penal Code
originalOptions: Medical Association Law + Public Health Law + Jordanian Penal Code
questions.correctAnswer: C) Medical Association Law + Public Health Law + Jordanian Penal Code
questions.correctAnswerText: Medical Association Law + Public Health Law + Jordanian Penal Code
questions.explanation: Jordanian physicians are bound by three combined legal frameworks: the Medical Association Law, the Public Health Law, and the Penal Code (governing criminal negligence).

questions.text: Hesitation marks are seen in:
questions.explanation: Hesitation marks are multiple shallow, parallel test cuts made before the fatal incision — characteristic of suicidal cut-throat/wrist injuries.

questions.text: In suicidal cut throats, we see:
questions.explanation: Suicidal cut-throats show progressive hesitation marks reflecting the "testing" phase before the fatal incision, unlike homicidal single deep wounds.

questions.text: Green color in a bruise is due to:
questions.explanation: Biliverdin production (~3–5 days post-injury) gives bruises their green color, following the red/blue → brown progression.

questions.text: Which is FALSE about abrasions?
options: Third healing stage involves granulation tissue
They indicate the direction of force
originalOptions: Third healing stage involves granulation tissue
They indicate the direction of force
questions.correctAnswer: B) Third healing stage involves granulation tissue
questions.correctAnswerText: Third healing stage involves granulation tissue
questions.explanation: Abrasions involve only the epidermis and heal by re-epithelialization, not granulation tissue — granulation is a deeper-wound healing feature, making this statement false.

questions.text: True about abrasion:
options: Even if it bleeds, it heals WITHOUT scarring
originalOptions: Even if it bleeds, it heals WITHOUT scarring
questions.correctAnswer: A) Even if it bleeds, it heals WITHOUT scarring
questions.correctAnswerText: Even if it bleeds, it heals WITHOUT scarring
questions.explanation: Because abrasions are epidermal-only injuries, they heal by re-epithelialization without significant scarring even if superficial bleeding occurs.

questions.text: The best type of injury for indicating the tool used:
questions.explanation: Patterned abrasions best reproduce the surface contour of the inflicting object (e.g., tyre marks, buckle imprints), making abrasions the most useful for tool identification.

questions.text: Importance of Langer's lines (Lines of Langerhans):
questions.explanation: Langer's lines reflect skin tension/collagen orientation; wounds parallel to them gape less, while perpendicular wounds gape widely.

questions.text: Clinical importance of Langer's lines in a wound:
options: Determines the depth of the wound
Determines the direction of hair growth
Determines the degree of gaping of an incised wound
originalOptions: Determines the depth of the wound
Determines the direction of hair growth
Determines the degree of gaping of an incised wound
questions.correctAnswer: D) Determines the degree of gaping of an incised wound
questions.correctAnswerText: Determines the degree of gaping of an incised wound
questions.explanation: The clinical value of Langer's lines is predicting the degree of gaping of an incised wound based on its orientation relative to skin tension lines.

questions.text: Crescent-shaped abrasions are caused by:
questions.explanation: Fingernails produce characteristic crescent (semi-lunar) shaped abrasions, distinct from the paired arcuate marks of teeth.

questions.text: The superficial layer of skin scraped off (tangential force) is called:
questions.explanation: A graze (brush) abrasion results from tangential force scraping off the superficial epidermis, as in road-rash type injuries.

questions.text: Graze abrasion is the same as:
questions.explanation: "Graze" and "brush" abrasion are synonymous terms for the same tangential scraping mechanism.

questions.text: Prominence abrasion is most commonly found in which area of the body?
questions.explanation: Over the scalp, skin is tightly applied to the underlying bone with minimal soft-tissue cushioning, allowing the clearest reproduction of a patterned abrasion.

questions.text: Patterned abrasion looks clearest when the injury is on the:
questions.explanation: Bony prominences like the scalp lack a soft-tissue cushion, so the weapon's surface pattern is reproduced most clearly there.

questions.text: NOT necessary to see a patterned abrasion:
questions.explanation: Subcutaneous fat cushions the blow and distorts the pattern, so its absence (not its presence) is what favors clear patterned abrasions — bone underneath is what's required.

questions.text: Incised-like lacerations can be seen in all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Incised-like lacerations occur where skin is crushed directly against underlying bone (scalp, eyebrow, shin); the chest wall has more soft-tissue cushioning, preventing this clean-split appearance.

questions.text: Blunt trauma can simulate an incised wound specifically over which part of the body:
questions.explanation: Blunt force over the thin, bone-backed scalp can split the skin cleanly enough to mimic an incised wound.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT TRUE concerning bruises:
options: Bruising is most commonly seen in the skin, but it NEVER occurs in the deeper tissues, including muscle and internal organs
The source of bleeding is usually small-caliber blood vessels such as veins and arterioles
Bruises are caused by leakage of blood into underlying tissues from damaged blood vessels
The size and appearance of a bruise is related to the site of the injured part of the body
Bruises are discoloration of the skin surface due to a blunt force instrument
originalOptions: Bruising is most commonly seen in the skin, but it NEVER occurs in the deeper tissues, including muscle and internal organs
The source of bleeding is usually small-caliber blood vessels such as veins and arterioles
Bruises are caused by leakage of blood into underlying tissues from damaged blood vessels
The size and appearance of a bruise is related to the site of the injured part of the body
Bruises are discoloration of the skin surface due to a blunt force instrument
questions.correctAnswer: A) Bruising is most commonly seen in the skin, but it NEVER occurs in the deeper tissues, including muscle and internal organs
questions.correctAnswerText: Bruising is most commonly seen in the skin, but it NEVER occurs in the deeper tissues, including muscle and internal organs
questions.explanation: Bruising is not confined to skin — it can and does occur in deep tissues, muscle, and internal organs (e.g., deep haematomas, organ contusions), making this statement false.

questions.text: Intradermal bruising is best described as:
questions.explanation: Intradermal bruising traps blood within the dermis, reproducing the pattern of the inflicting object — the most forensically informative type of bruise.

questions.text: One of the following is TRUE concerning laceration:
options: Laceration is always connected to intentional violent acts
Lacerations appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
The more resilient tissues will always be damaged by the forces that split the other weaker tissues
They appear as the result of a sharp object against skin
originalOptions: Laceration is always connected to intentional violent acts
Lacerations appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
The more resilient tissues will always be damaged by the forces that split the other weaker tissues
They appear as the result of a sharp object against skin
questions.correctAnswer: B) Lacerations appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
questions.correctAnswerText: Lacerations appear as cuts, splits or tears in the skin
questions.explanation: Lacerations are defined as tears/splits in the skin from blunt force, with irregular edges and surrounding bruising — not from sharp objects.

questions.text: NOT true regarding a lacerated wound:
questions.explanation: While lacerations are usually irregular, those over bony prominences (scalp, shin) can appear deceptively regular/incised-like, so "always irregular" is not strictly true.

questions.text: Blunt instruments/weapons can usually cause all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Sharp, clean-cut edges are a feature of sharp-weapon injuries, not blunt trauma, which instead produces abrasions, contusions, and ragged lacerations.

questions.text: One of the following is NOT characteristic of self-inflicted injuries:
options: Injuries are grouped on the contralateral side to the patient's common hand use
On an area of the body that the individual can access themselves
originalOptions: Injuries are grouped on the contralateral side to the patient's common hand use
On an area of the body that the individual can access themselves
questions.correctAnswer: A) Usually multiple and deep wounds
questions.explanation: Self-inflicted wounds are typically superficial and tentative (hesitation marks); multiple deep wounds instead suggest homicidal or accidental injury.

questions.text: Fabricated wounds are mostly:
questions.explanation: Fabricated (self-inflicted for secondary gain) wounds are usually incised, made with a sharp object on visible, accessible areas.

questions.text: Which is the most frequent type of wound seen in DEFENSE wounds:
questions.explanation: Defense wounds are most often cut/incised injuries sustained when the victim grabs or deflects a blade.

questions.text: Defense wounds are most likely seen in:
options: Back of hands / dorsum of forearms
originalOptions: Back of hands / dorsum of forearms
questions.correctAnswer: A) Back of hands / dorsum of forearms
questions.correctAnswerText: Back of hands / dorsum of forearms
questions.explanation: Classic defense wound sites are the ulnar border and dorsum of the forearms/hands, raised instinctively to shield the face and neck.

questions.text: Hesitation wound – which is NOT correct:
questions.explanation: Hesitation marks are superficial, parallel, regular-edged tentative cuts — they are not surrounded by bruising, which would instead suggest blunt trauma.

questions.text: Yellow discoloration of a bruise is expected at approximately what time?
questions.explanation: Bilirubin formation from degraded haemoglobin typically produces the yellow discoloration of a bruise around 5–7 days post-injury.

questions.text: Common cause of death in extradural hemorrhage:
questions.explanation: Extradural hemorrhage causes rapid mass effect and brainstem herniation, leading to death primarily from respiratory centre failure.

questions.text: What is the main characteristic of the wound shown in the image? [img: forensic1stabwound.jpg ]
options: Ragged, irregular edges with tissue bridging
Sharp, clean edges with regular margins and no surrounding bruising
Diffuse bruising with poorly defined margins
originalOptions: Ragged, irregular edges with tissue bridging
Sharp, clean edges with regular margins and no surrounding bruising
Diffuse bruising with poorly defined margins
questions.correctAnswer: B) Sharp, clean edges with regular margins and no surrounding bruising
questions.correctAnswerText: Sharp, clean edges with regular margins and no surrounding bruising
questions.explanation: Stab/incised wounds show sharp, clean, regular margins with minimal surrounding tissue damage, distinguishing them from the ragged, bruised margins of lacerations.

questions.text: Concerning stab wounds, one of the following statements is NOT correct:
options: A slit-like wound will usually distort after removal of the weapon
An irregularly-shaped skin wound may result if the knife is twisted
Movement of the knife may cause wound enlargement
One wound apex is sharp if the weapon is single sharp-edged
The resulting defect of the edges is usually the exact size as the knife
originalOptions: A slit-like wound will usually distort after removal of the weapon
An irregularly-shaped skin wound may result if the knife is twisted
Movement of the knife may cause wound enlargement
One wound apex is sharp if the weapon is single sharp-edged
The resulting defect of the edges is usually the exact size as the knife
questions.correctAnswer: E) The resulting defect of the edges is usually the exact size as the knife
questions.correctAnswerText: The resulting defect of the edges is usually the exact size as the knife
questions.explanation: Skin elasticity, wound-edge retraction, and any blade movement mean the resulting skin defect is rarely the exact size of the knife, even when edges are approximated.

questions.text: A fully conscious person sustained a head injury during a fight. Boggy swelling 6x4 cm on the right parietal area. X-ray showed a fracture of the parietal bone without displacement. The nature of the injury is:
questions.explanation: A single linear fracture without bone displacement is classified as a fissure (linear) fracture, distinct from depressed or comminuted patterns.

questions.text: A skull fracture with multiple bone fragments is termed:
questions.explanation: A comminuted (fragmented) skull fracture is defined by multiple bone fragments, as opposed to a single linear fissure line.

questions.text: A burn that is full-thickness and painless due to nerve destruction is classified as:
questions.explanation: Full-thickness skin destruction with loss of sensation (due to nerve destruction) defines a 3rd-degree burn, distinguishing it from the painful, blistering 2nd-degree burn.

questions.text: In a gunshot wound case during surgery, the correct approach regarding the bullet is:
options: Remove and discard the bullet immediately to prevent further injury
Treat the wound; preserve the bullet in situ if possible; document; do NOT discard it
The bullet is the surgeon's property
The bullet must be handed to the patient's family
originalOptions: Remove and discard the bullet immediately to prevent further injury
Treat the wound; preserve the bullet in situ if possible; document; do NOT discard it
The bullet is the surgeon's property
The bullet must be handed to the patient's family
questions.correctAnswer: B) Treat the wound; preserve the bullet in situ if possible; document; do NOT discard it
questions.correctAnswerText: Treat the wound; preserve the bullet in situ if possible; document; do NOT discard it
questions.explanation: A retrieved bullet is critical ballistic evidence — it must be preserved in situ where possible, handled carefully, documented, and never discarded.

allQuestions.text: Under Jordanian law, abortion is permitted under which of the following circumstances?
options: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
originalOptions: When requested by the mother for personal reasons
When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
Up to 12 weeks of gestation for any reason
allQuestions.correctAnswer: B) When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
allQuestions.correctAnswerText: When continuing the pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life or health
allQuestions.explanation: Jordanian law criminalizes abortion except when continuing the pregnancy would seriously endanger the mother's life or health; it is not permitted on demand, for socioeconomic reasons, or for fetal anomaly alone.

allQuestions.text: Abortion in Jordanian law is allowed:
options: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
originalOptions: Up to 12 weeks for any reason
allQuestions.correctAnswer: E) To save the mother's life
allQuestions.explanation: Under the Jordan Penal Code, abortion is a criminal offense except when continuation of pregnancy poses a serious risk to the mother's life.

allQuestions.text: Which of the following is NOT a cause or indicator of child abuse?
allQuestions.explanation: MS is a neurological autoimmune disease unrelated to abuse; multiple bruises, shaken baby syndrome, and Munchausen by proxy are classic abuse indicators.

allQuestions.text: Bruising in which of the following areas is NOT considered a suspicious sign of child abuse?
allQuestions.explanation: Knee bruising is a common, normal childhood injury from falls and play; abuse-related bruising is characteristically found on protected areas such as the torso, back, abdomen, and chest.

allQuestions.text: Regarding Munchausen syndrome by proxy, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
options: Illness does not suggest a particular disease
The child becomes ill in the presence of the caregiver
Laboratory and radiographic findings are negative
